title: Standards-Compliant Isn't the Same as Clinically Correct
description: An AI-generated FHIR resource can pass every conformance check — correct resource type, correct LOINC code, correctly structured reference range — and still attach clinical parameters that are wrong for this specific patient.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish HL7/FHIR structural conformance from clinical correctness of the data a message carries
Identify a case where a schema-valid FHIR resource carries a clinically inappropriate value

contentSections.title: Validating Against Real Standards

contentSections.body: An AI-assisted lab pipeline converts an HL7 v2 result message into a FHIR Observation resource for a 4-year-old patient's creatinine test. The resulting resource is schema-valid: correct resource type, correct LOINC code, correct units, a properly structured `referenceRange` element. Every field a FHIR conformance validator checks passes. The problem is upstream of the schema: the reference range attached is the standard adult range, not a pediatric one — and a creatinine value that's clearly elevated relative to a young child's much smaller muscle mass reads as comfortably 'within range' against adult numbers. The message is fully standards-compliant. The clinical interpretation is wrong, and nothing about FHIR conformance checking would catch it, because which reference population to use is configuration data, not a structural requirement the standard enforces.

contentSections.question: Before the mechanism — the conformance validator reports zero errors on this Observation. What would you check first yourself?
contentSections.answer: Whether the clinical parameters attached to the value fit this patient. Here that means the reference range: the resource carries the standard adult range for a 4-year-old. The validator confirmed structure — resource type, LOINC code, units, a properly formed `referenceRange` element — and none of those checks look at who the patient is.
contentSections.hint: The validator checked the shape of the resource. What did it never look at?

contentSections.body:
HL7 and FHIR conformance validation checks *structure*: is this the right resource type, are required elements present, is the coding system correct (LOINC, SNOMED CT), are data types right. None of that requires understanding the patient in front of you. HIPAA sits on a separate axis entirely — privacy and security controls, not clinical accuracy — so a message can be fully HIPAA-compliant and fully HL7/FHIR-conformant and still carry a clinically wrong interpretation, because neither standard was built to check that.

The skill this module trains is checking a third thing neither standard touches: does the specific clinical context of *this patient* — age, weight, sex, relevant history — match the reference parameters the system attached. A pipeline that's technically correct on both standards can still silently apply the wrong population's normal range, and that failure mode is invisible to anyone only checking conformance.

contentSections.scenario: Two compliance layers have already signed off on this record: FHIR conformance validation reported zero errors, and the exchange met HIPAA privacy and security requirements.
contentSections.question: Select every check those two layers actually performed.

items.label: Is this the correct FHIR resource type
Are the required elements present
Is the coding system correct (LOINC, SNOMED CT)
Are the data types right
Are privacy and security controls in place
Is the attached reference range the right one for a 4-year-old
Does this result read correctly for this particular patient

explanation.resource-type: Yes — resource type is core structural conformance.
explanation.required-elements: Yes. Presence of required elements is exactly what conformance validation is for.
explanation.coding-system: Yes — the validator checks that codes come from the expected terminology.
explanation.data-types: Yes. Structural again, and entirely independent of the patient.
explanation.privacy-controls: Yes, but on a separate axis. HIPAA covers privacy and security, not whether the clinical content is right.
explanation.range-for-age: No. Which reference population applies is configuration data, not a structural requirement the standard enforces — so a correctly-formed `referenceRange` element passes regardless of which range it carries.
explanation.value-interpretation: No. How the result reads depends on which reference population applies, which is the thing neither layer checks. Against adult numbers this value sits comfortably in range; that is the failure, and no validator has an opinion on it.

contentSections.synthesis: Both layers check real things, and neither checks the thing you do. Conformance covers structure, HIPAA covers privacy and security, and whether the clinical parameters fit this patient is a third axis with no validator behind it.

contentSections.scenario: FHIR Observation resource for a 4-year-old patient: LOINC code correct, units correct, value present, `referenceRange` element correctly structured and populated — but with the standard adult reference range rather than an age-appropriate pediatric one. A FHIR conformance validator reports zero errors.
contentSections.question: Why does this resource pass conformance validation despite carrying a clinically inappropriate reference range?

options.label: Conformance validation checks that the resource is well-formed and uses correct codes — it has no concept of which reference population is clinically appropriate for this patient
This resource is actually invalid FHIR and the validator should have caught it
The LOINC code must be the wrong one if the interpretation is wrong

feedback.conformance-checks-structure-not-populat: Correct. FHIR conformance validation confirms structural correctness — resource type, required elements, coding systems — none of which encodes 'is this the right reference range for a 4-year-old.' That's a clinical-context judgment layered on top of a structurally valid message, which is exactly the gap this track trains you to catch.
feedback.resource-is-actually-invalid: The resource is structurally valid FHIR — correct resource type, correct required elements, correct coding system. Its clinical inappropriateness doesn't make it non-conformant; conformance and clinical correctness are separate axes, which is the whole point of this lesson.
feedback.loinc-code-is-wrong: The LOINC code correctly identifies the test being performed (creatinine). The problem isn't which test was coded — it's which reference population was used to interpret the resulting value, an entirely separate piece of configuration data.

contentSections.mechanism: HL7/FHIR conformance and HIPAA compliance both validate real, necessary things — interoperable structure and privacy/security controls, respectively — but neither checks whether the specific clinical parameters (like a reference range) attached to a value are appropriate for the actual patient. That gap is exactly where a standards-compliant record can still be clinically wrong.

contentSections.intro: Write up the finding on this Observation resource. Three fields, each of which has to state what is actually true rather than what is convenient.

fields.prompt: What did the FHIR conformance validator report?

options.label: passed, zero errors
failed, invalid structure

feedback.passed - zero errors: Right, and recording it matters. A finding that omits the clean conformance result invites someone to re-run the validator and conclude there is nothing here.
feedback.failed - invalid structure: The resource is structurally valid FHIR — correct resource type, correct required elements, correct coding system. Writing it up as a structural failure sends it to the wrong team and gets it closed as unreproducible.

fields.prompt: What is actually wrong with the resource?

options.label: wrong LOINC code for the test performed
options.value: wrong LOINC code for the test performed

options.label: adult reference range attached for a 4-year-old patient
options.value: adult reference range attached for a 4-year-old patient

options.label: required element missing from the resource
options.value: required element missing from the resource

fields.correctValue: adult reference range attached for a 4-year-old patient

feedback.wrong LOINC code for the test performed: The LOINC code correctly identifies the test that was performed. Which test was coded is not the problem; which population's range was used to interpret the result is.
feedback.adult reference range attached for a 4-y: Right. The reference range is present, correctly structured, and drawn from the wrong population for this patient — a clinical-context error sitting on top of a structurally sound resource.
feedback.required element missing from the resour: The `referenceRange` element is present and correctly structured, which is part of why conformance passed. The failure is in which range it carries, not whether it is there.

fields.prompt: Which layer could have caught this?

options.label: FHIR conformance validation
HIPAA security review
human review of clinical context against the patient
options.value: human review of clinical context against the patient

fields.correctValue: human review of clinical context against the patient

feedback.FHIR conformance validation: It already ran and reported zero errors. Sending this back to conformance validation asks a structural check to answer a clinical question it has no concept of.
feedback.HIPAA security review: HIPAA sits on the privacy and security axis. A perfectly secured record can carry a clinically wrong interpretation, and nothing in that review would surface it.
feedback.human review of clinical context against: Right — comparing the attached parameters against the patient's actual age is the check neither standard performs, and the reason this review layer exists.

contentSections.synthesis: Written out, the finding is unambiguous: structurally sound, properly secured, clinically wrong. Those three fields are independent of each other, and a record can pass the first two every single time while still needing the third.

contentSections.body: Passing HL7/FHIR conformance and HIPAA compliance tells you a record is structurally sound and properly secured — it tells you nothing about whether the clinical parameters attached to that structure (reference ranges, population defaults) match the actual patient. That's the specific check this module trains, and no standards validator performs it for you.

title: Clinically Accurate Isn't the Same as Standards-Conformant Either
description: The previous lesson showed standards-compliant-but-clinically-wrong. The failure runs the other way too: a note that's completely accurate in plain language can still fail FHIR conformance if it's not expressed in machine-actionable, coded form.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize that FHIR requires machine-actionable coded identifiers, not narrative text, for structural fields
Identify a FHIR resource that is clinically accurate but structurally non-conformant

contentSections.title: Validating Against Real Standards

contentSections.body: An AI-generated FHIR `Condition` resource has `Condition.code` populated with only `text: "Type 2 diabetes with nephropathy"` — no `coding` array, no ICD-10-CM or SNOMED CT entry, just a plain-text description. To a human reading the record, this is completely accurate: that's exactly what the patient has. Against a profile like US Core, which requires `Condition.code` to carry a coded value from a specified terminology, this resource fails conformance. The previous lesson's failure mode was standards-compliant-but-clinically-wrong. This one is the mirror image: clinically accurate, structurally non-conformant.

FHIR's whole purpose is interoperability — different systems reliably exchanging and machine-processing clinical data, not just displaying it to a human reader. That requires certain fields to carry *coded*, machine-resolvable values rather than free-text descriptions, even when the free text is perfectly understandable to a person. `Condition.code` with only `text` populated isn't wrong information — the description is accurate — but it's information in a form a coded profile doesn't recognize as structurally valid, because a downstream system consuming this record has no reliable way to match, aggregate, or act on plain text the way it can a real ICD-10-CM or SNOMED CT entry.

This matters for review work specifically because it's tempting to treat "the content is medically accurate" as the whole check. It isn't. A record can be entirely true and still fail the structural requirements a profile imposes — and catching that requires checking the *form* the information takes, not just whether the information itself is correct.

contentSections.scenario: The Condition resource from this lesson: `Condition.code.text` reads "Type 2 diabetes with nephropathy", `Condition.code.coding` is empty, and every other element matches the source documentation.
contentSections.question: Select every statement that is true of this resource.

items.label: The clinical content is accurate
It fails a profile that requires a coded Condition.code
A downstream system can't reliably match or aggregate it
Condition.code is optional in base FHIR R4
The diagnosis it describes is medically wrong
More detailed free text would satisfy the profile

explanation.content-accurate: True. The description matches what the patient has — that is what lets this failure mode slip through a review.
explanation.fails-profile: True. A profile that requires a coded value is not satisfied by text, however accurate the text is.
explanation.not-machine-actionable: True. Plain text can be displayed to a person, but the next system in the pipeline has no reliable way to match, aggregate, or act on it.
explanation.optional-in-base: True, and it is the detail that makes this confusing. Base FHIR R4 leaves Condition.code optional; the profile narrows that and requires a coded value when the field is used.
explanation.diagnosis-wrong: False. The clinical content is accurate and matches the documentation. The failure is entirely about the form the information takes.
explanation.more-text-fixes: False. The requirement is for an entry from a coded terminology, not for a better description. Text of any quality still isn't a code.

contentSections.synthesis: Four of these are true at once, which is the uncomfortable part: accurate content, an optional base field, a stricter profile, and a real conformance failure. A review that asked only whether the record was true would have cleared it.

contentSections.code:
FHIR Condition resource, evaluated against a profile (e.g. US Core) requiring a coded Condition.code:
Condition.code.text = "Type 2 diabetes with nephropathy"
Condition.code.coding = [] (empty — no ICD-10-CM or SNOMED CT entry)

All clinical content in the resource (diagnosis, dates, patient reference) is accurate and matches the source documentation.
contentSections.question: Why does this resource fail conformance against a profile requiring a coded Condition.code, despite being clinically accurate?

options.label: Condition.code carries only free text, no entry from a coded terminology (ICD-10-CM, SNOMED CT) — a profile requiring a coded value isn't satisfied by text alone, regardless of how accurate that text is
The diagnosis described must be clinically incorrect if the resource fails conformance
Condition.code is entirely optional in FHIR R4, so any content in it, coded or not, is acceptable

feedback.text-only-not-coded: Correct. A profile that constrains Condition.code to require a coded value needs an actual entry from a specified terminology — text alone, however accurate, doesn't satisfy that structural requirement. This is a real conformance failure independent of clinical correctness, which is exactly why 'the content is medically accurate' isn't a sufficient review check on its own.
feedback.diagnosis-itself-wrong: The scenario states the clinical content is accurate and matches documentation. The conformance failure is specifically about the structural form of Condition.code — missing a coded entry — not about whether the diagnosis itself is correct.
feedback.code-field-optional: In base FHIR R4, Condition.code is indeed optional (0..1) — but the scenario specifies a profile like US Core, which narrows that base cardinality and requires a coded value when the field is used. A profile can impose stricter rules than the base specification, which is exactly what's happening here.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Free text and coded terminology look interchangeable to a human reader — both describe the same real diagnosis — but only a coded entry is machine-actionable: matchable, aggregatable, and processable by the next system in an interoperability pipeline. A profile requiring a coded value is enforcing that machine-actionability, not double-checking clinical accuracy the base FHIR spec already assumes. Catching this requires checking which specific profile applies and whether its stricter requirements are met, not just reading whether the resource is medically true.

contentSections.intro: Write up this resource as a review finding. Both halves of the verdict have to appear, or the next person reads it as a pass.

fields.prompt: What is the verdict on the clinical content?

options.label: inaccurate, contradicts the documentation
accurate, matches the documentation

feedback.inaccurate - contradicts the source docu: The content is accurate — diagnosis, dates, and patient reference all match the source. Recording it as inaccurate sends a clinician chasing a clinical error that isn't there.
feedback.accurate - matches the source documentat: Right, and stating it plainly is what keeps the finding honest. The resource is true; that is not the whole check.

fields.prompt: What is the verdict on conformance?

options.label: fails, Condition.code carries no coded entry
options.value: fails - Condition.code carries no coded entry

options.label: passes, the text is sufficient

fields.correctValue: fails - Condition.code carries no coded entry

feedback.fails - Condition.code carries no coded: Right. Naming the specific element and what it lacks is what makes the finding actionable rather than a general complaint about quality.
feedback.passes - the text is sufficient: Text is sufficient for a human reader, not for a profile that constrains Condition.code to a coded value. Marking this as a pass leaves a non-conformant resource in the pipeline.

options.label: rewrite the free text more precisely
options.value: rewrite the free text more precisely

options.label: add a coded terminology entry to Condition.code
options.value: add a coded terminology entry to Condition.code

options.label: remove Condition.code from the resource

fields.correctValue: add a coded terminology entry to Condition.code

feedback.rewrite the free text more precisely: Precision of the description was never the issue. The profile wants a coded, machine-resolvable value, and better prose does not become one.
feedback.add a coded terminology entry to Conditi: Right — supply the coded value the profile requires (ICD-10-CM or SNOMED CT, per the applicable profile). The existing text can stay; it just can't stand alone.
feedback.remove Condition.code from the resource: Removing the field deletes accurate clinical information and still doesn't satisfy a profile that requires a coded value in it.

contentSections.synthesis: The finding carries both halves. Accurate and non-conformant are not in tension here — they are two independent verdicts, and a write-up that reports only one of them is incomplete.

contentSections.scenario:
Two resources from this module.

**A** — Observation for a 4-year-old: correct resource type, correct LOINC code, correct units, a correctly structured `referenceRange` carrying the standard adult range.

**B** — Condition: accurate diagnosis in `Condition.code.text`, empty `coding` array, evaluated against a profile that requires a coded value.
contentSections.question: Which of these fails a conformance validator?

options.label: B only
A only
Both
Neither

feedback.b-only: Correct. B is missing a coded value the profile requires, so it fails conformance while being clinically accurate. A is structurally flawless and clinically wrong for this patient. Opposite failures — only one of them is a conformance failure.
feedback.a-only: Reversed. A's problem, an adult reference range on a 4-year-old, is invisible to conformance checking, because which reference population applies isn't a structural requirement. B's problem is the structural one.
feedback.both: A passes. Everything a conformance validator checks on A is correct: resource type, LOINC code, units, `referenceRange` structure. Its problem sits outside what conformance covers.
feedback.neither: B fails. A profile requiring a coded `Condition.code` is not satisfied by text alone, no matter how accurate that text is.

contentSections.concept: Structural conformance and clinical correctness are independent axes, and a record can fail on either one by itself. Checking only conformance clears A; checking only whether the content is true clears B. Review work means running both checks separately and never letting a pass on one stand in for the other.

contentSections.body: Reviewing for correctness means checking two independent things: is the clinical content accurate, and is it expressed in the structural form the applicable profile actually requires. A resource can pass one check and fail the other in either direction — this lesson's failure mode is the mirror of the previous one, and catching both requires checking form and content separately, not assuming one implies the other.

title: Why standards exist: the message that has to survive the trip
description: What HL7 and FHIR actually standardize — the shared syntax and coded vocabulary that let two systems that have never spoken to each other exchange a record without losing or misreading it — and what they were never built to check.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a data-exchange standard guarantees and what it doesn't
Distinguish a syntax/parsing failure from a semantics/coding failure

contentSections.title: The trip a message takes

contentSections.body: Riverside Memorial discharges a patient on Epic. The discharge summary — three new medications, one updated allergy — has to reach Dr. Okafor's outpatient practice, running athenahealth, a system built by a different company that has never seen Riverside's internal data model. If the two systems don't agree, field for field, on what "medication" means and where it lives in the message, the note either fails to render at Dr. Okafor's end, or worse, renders with the allergy update silently missing.

HL7 (Health Level 7) is the standards body, and it has produced two exchange formats you'll meet in this module. **HL7 v2**, dating to 1987, is still the workhorse for high-volume real-time feeds — lab results, admit/discharge/transfer events, orders — sent as pipe-delimited text messages over a persistent connection between two systems' interface engines. **FHIR** (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), the newer standard most new work targets, represents the same clinical facts as discrete, RESTful "resources" exchanged as JSON or XML over HTTP, closer to how a modern web API works. Most health systems run both at once: v2 still carrying the real-time plumbing, FHIR carrying the newer patient-portal and app-facing API surface, often required under the interoperability rules that came out of the 21st Century Cures Act.

What either standard actually guarantees is narrower than it sounds: a shared **syntax** (where a field starts and ends, what character separates one field from the next) and a shared **vocabulary binding** (this field's value has to come from this specific code system — ICD-10-CM, LOINC, SNOMED CT). Neither guarantees that the value chosen from that vocabulary is the *right* one for this patient. That gap is what the rest of this module trains you to close.

contentSections.scenario:
Two integration complaints land on the same engineering ticket in the same week.

**Complaint 1:** A cardiology practice's new lab interface stops delivering results entirely — the receiving system throws a parse error and drops the message.

**Complaint 2:** The same interface delivers results that parse and display fine, but a weight-based dosing alert never fires, because the medication's dose unit arrived coded as `mg` when the ordering system actually meant `mcg` for that particular drug — a real prescribing error, not a transmission error.
contentSections.question: Which of these is the kind of failure a data-exchange standard like HL7/FHIR is built to prevent?

options.label: Both — a standard exists to guarantee the message content is clinically correct

Only Complaint 1 — the parse failure is a syntax problem the standard's structure exists to prevent; Complaint 2 is a real clinical error that happened before the message was ever built, and no data standard catches that
Neither — both are the receiving system's fault for not validating harder

feedback.both: A standard can guarantee the message's shape and that a field's value comes from an agreed code system — it has no way to know whether the human or system that populated the field made a correct clinical decision before the message was ever assembled. Unit-of-measure confusion at the point of prescribing is exactly that kind of error: the message is a faithful, standards-conformant carrier of a mistake that already existed.
feedback.syntax: Right. Complaint 1 is precisely what a shared syntax exists to prevent — two systems agreeing on field boundaries and delimiters so a message that leaves one system is parseable at the other. Complaint 2 is a clinical/prescribing error the message correctly transported; the standard's job ended at delivering the field faithfully, not at catching that the field's content was wrong before it was ever sent.
feedback.neither: The receiving system did validate — that's exactly why Complaint 1 threw a parse error instead of silently corrupting data. Complaint 2 isn't a validation failure either; a correctly-coded `mg` value that should have been `mcg` is a decision error upstream of any message, and nothing about receiving-side validation would have known which unit was intended.

contentSections.concept: **A standard is built to make sure the message that left one system is the message that arrives at the other — structurally intact and drawing its codes from an agreed vocabulary.** It was never built to confirm that what's inside the message is clinically true. That's a second, separate job, and it's the one this module trains.

contentSections.title: What HL7 and FHIR actually standardize

contentSections.body: A hospital's interface engine, in 2026, is quietly running both standards on the same patient at once: HL7 v2.5.1 ORU messages stream lab results from the core lab system to the EHR in real time, the way they have for two decades, while a FHIR R4 API serves that same patient's results out to their portal app the moment they're finalized. Neither is being phased out on any near-term timeline — they're solving overlapping but not identical problems.

contentSections.scenario: Interface engineers estimate that the large majority of a typical US hospital's real-time clinical data feeds — lab results, admit/discharge/transfer events, orders — still run over legacy HL7 v2 connections rather than FHIR, even at organizations with a fully modern FHIR-based patient app layered on top.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of those real-time feeds still run on HL7 v2 rather than FHIR, in a typical hospital's interface engine today?
contentSections.explanation: This figure is illustrative, not a number to memorize — it varies by organization and changes year to year. The shape of it is what matters: FHIR has not replaced v2 for high-volume, real-time internal plumbing; it's been layered on top, primarily for API-style access (patient apps, external partner integrations, the kind of access the Cures Act API rule specifically targets). A reviewer working this pipeline should expect to meet both, often on the same patient in the same afternoon, not assume v2 is a thing of the past.

contentSections.body: A standard's job is making sure the message that left one system is the message that arrives at the other — not making sure what's inside it was true to begin with.

title: FHIR resources: Patient, Encounter, Condition, Observation
description: The four FHIR resource types that carry most of what a reviewer checks — what each one is for, its key fields, and which chart fact belongs in which resource.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the purpose and key fields of Patient, Encounter, Condition, and Observation resources
Map a chart fact to the FHIR resource type it belongs in

contentSections.title: The four you'll live in

contentSections.body: An AI pipeline assembles a FHIR bundle for a sprained-ankle ED visit: eleven resources total, but four resource types carry almost the entire clinical story — who the patient is, what encounter happened, what was diagnosed, and what was measured.

**Patient** carries identity: `identifier`, `name`, `birthDate`, `gender`, `address`. You rarely edit this resource directly, but its `birthDate` and `gender` are what other resources' clinical context depends on — a pediatric reference range only makes sense once you've confirmed the linked Patient's age.

**Encounter** carries the visit itself: `status` (planned/in-progress/finished), `class` (a coded value — `AMB` ambulatory, `EMER` emergency, `IMP` inpatient, `OBSENC` observation), `period.start`/`period.end`, and `subject` (a reference to the Patient). Get the `class` wrong — code an overnight observation stay as `AMB` — and every downstream billing and utilization decision inherits the error.

**Condition** carries a diagnosis or problem: `clinicalStatus` (active/resolved/remission), `verificationStatus` (confirmed/provisional/differential), `code` (bound to ICD-10-CM or SNOMED CT), `subject`, `encounter`, and `onsetDateTime`.

**Observation** carries a measured or reported fact: `status`, `code` (bound to LOINC), `value[x]` (the actual result — a quantity, a coded value, a string), `subject`, `encounter`, `effectiveDateTime`, and often a `referenceRange`. Vitals, labs, and most exam findings live here.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a Condition resource for a straightforward chart fact: "Assessment: Type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications, active, confirmed diagnosis, addressed at today's follow-up."

feedback.active: Right — the note describes an ongoing condition being actively managed, not one that has resolved or that recurred after resolution.
feedback.resolved: "Resolved" is for a condition that's over — T2DM being followed and managed is the definition of active, not resolved.
feedback.recurrence: Recurrence implies the condition had previously resolved and has now come back — nothing in this note suggests that history.

feedback.confirmed: Right — the note states this as a settled diagnosis, not a working hypothesis.
feedback.provisional: Provisional is for a diagnosis still being worked up — this note presents T2DM as an established, ongoing diagnosis, not a candidate.
feedback.differential: Differential implies multiple competing diagnoses under consideration — nothing here suggests that.

fields.prompt: Which code system should Condition.code draw from for a billable diagnosis in a US claim?

feedback.ICD-10-CM: Right — ICD-10-CM is the diagnosis code set US claims require; Condition.code is commonly bound to it directly, or to SNOMED CT with an ICD-10-CM mapping layered on for billing.
feedback.CPT: CPT codes procedures and services, not diagnoses — that belongs on a Procedure resource, not Condition.code.
feedback.RxNorm: RxNorm codes medications, not diagnoses — it has no role in Condition.code.

contentSections.synthesis: A Condition resource for this fact: `clinicalStatus: active`, `verificationStatus: confirmed`, `code` carrying E11.9 from ICD-10-CM, `subject` referencing this patient, `encounter` referencing today's visit.

contentSections.title: Which resource a chart fact belongs in

contentSections.body: ED note: "62F presents with 3 days of productive cough. Temp 101.4°F, O2 sat 94% on room air. Diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia. Admitted to observation."

Four sentences, four different resource types. The patient's age and sex populate fields already on the **Patient** resource (or confirm them, if the Patient resource predates this visit — it usually does). "Admitted to observation" sets the **Encounter**'s `class` to `OBSENC` and its `period`. The temperature and oxygen saturation are each a separate **Observation** — temperature bound to LOINC 8310-5, O2 sat bound to LOINC 2708-6, each carrying its own `value` and `effectiveDateTime`. "Community-acquired pneumonia" becomes a **Condition**, coded J18.9 (pneumonia, organism unspecified) in ICD-10-CM or SNOMED CT 233604007, with `encounter` referencing this same visit.

The skill isn't memorizing which resource type owns which field — it's reading a chart fact and immediately knowing which of the four questions it answers: *who* (Patient), *when-and-where* (Encounter), *what's-wrong* (Condition), or *what-was-measured* (Observation). An AI pipeline that puts a measured fact where a diagnosis belongs, or vice versa, is a structural error you're positioned to catch before you even get to whether the code inside is right.

contentSections.scenario: The same ED note: "62F presents with 3 days of productive cough. Temp 101.4°F, O2 sat 94% on room air. Diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia. Admitted to observation."
contentSections.question: Select every fact from this note that belongs on an Observation resource (as opposed to Patient, Encounter, or Condition).

items.label: Temp 101.4°F
O2 sat 94% on room air
62F (age and sex)
Community-acquired pneumonia (the diagnosis)
Admitted to observation

explanation.temp: Right — a measured vital sign with its own timestamp and LOINC code (8310-5), a textbook Observation.
explanation.o2: Right — same reasoning: a discrete measured value, LOINC 2708-6, another Observation.
explanation.age: Age and sex are Patient-level demographic facts, not a measurement taken at this encounter.
explanation.dx: Pneumonia is a diagnostic conclusion, not a measured value — it's a Condition, even though it was reached by interpreting some of these same Observations.
explanation.admit: The admission itself describes the visit's type and status — that's Encounter, not Observation.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of the five facts are measurements; the rest are demographic, diagnostic, or encounter-level facts that only look similar because they're all sitting in the same paragraph of the note.

contentSections.body: Four resource types, four different questions: who, when-and-where, what's-wrong, what-was-measured. Misfiling a fact into the wrong one is a structural error you can catch before you ever get to whether the code inside is right.

title: References between resources, and the broken ones
description: How FHIR resources point at each other — subject, encounter, and basedOn references — and the three ways those references break silently: dangling, cross-patient, and stale.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how FHIR resources reference one another and why cardinality rules matter
Identify a dangling, cross-patient, or stale reference in a bundle

contentSections.title: A bundle is a graph, not a list

contentSections.body: A 40-resource discharge bundle looks, at a glance, like a flat list of records. It isn't — it's a graph. The Condition resource for today's pneumonia diagnosis doesn't stand alone; it points at a Patient and, usually, at an Encounter. If that Encounter reference silently points at last month's ED visit for a sprained wrist instead of today's admission, the diagnosis attaches to the wrong visit — structurally valid, silently wrong.

A FHIR reference is a small JSON object naming another resource by type and id: `"subject": {"reference": "Patient/1204"}`. Cardinality rules govern how many references a field expects and whether they're required: `Condition.subject` is `1..1` — exactly one, required. `Condition.encounter` is `0..1` — optional, but a diagnosis addressed at a specific visit should carry it.

References break in three specific, common ways, and none of them throw a conformance error, because a reference that's syntactically well-formed satisfies the validator completely regardless of whether it points at the right thing:

1. **Dangling** — the reference names an id that doesn't exist in the bundle or the source system (a typo, or a resource dropped during assembly).
2. **Cross-patient** — the reference resolves to a real resource, but one belonging to a different patient than the resource pointing at it (a Condition's `subject` says Patient/1204, its `encounter` resolves to an Encounter whose own `subject` says Patient/1512).
3. **Stale** — the reference resolves, and to the right patient, but to the wrong visit — an old encounter instead of today's.

contentSections.question: What's the defect, and would a standard FHIR conformance validator catch it?

options.label: No defect — both resources are individually well-formed

A cross-patient reference: the Condition's subject is Patient/4489, but the Encounter it references belongs to Patient/5512 — and a conformance validator would not catch this, because both references are individually well-formed
A dangling reference — Encounter/77291 doesn't exist anywhere in the bundle

feedback.none: Look at the two `subject` values across the two resources — they name different patients. That's a real, if silent, structural problem.
feedback.cross: Right. Each resource, read alone, is perfectly well-formed — valid resource types, valid required fields, a reference that resolves to something real. The defect only shows up when you cross-check: the Condition says it belongs to Patient/4489, but the Encounter it's attached to belongs to Patient/5512. A conformance validator checks each resource's own shape and that references point at existing ids; it has no built-in expectation that a Condition's subject and its encounter's subject should match, because nothing in the FHIR spec structurally requires that check — it's a semantic consistency rule, not a syntax rule.
feedback.dangling: Encounter/77291 does exist — it's shown right there in the bundle. The problem isn't that the reference points at nothing; it's that it points at something real belonging to the wrong patient.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the shape of error that makes cross-checking references worth the extra minute: nothing about either resource alone is wrong. Only reading both and comparing subjects reveals that a diagnosis has been silently attached to the wrong patient's encounter — which, left uncaught, could mean a pneumonia diagnosis lands on the wrong chart entirely.

contentSections.title: Chasing a reference to see if it resolves

contentSections.body: An AI-assembled Observation resource for today's potassium level carries `"encounter": {"reference": "Encounter/62310"}`. Before trusting the value's context — which reference range applies, which visit this result should influence — the reference has to actually be chased down, not just glanced at.

Chasing a reference is a short, repeatable procedure, and it's closer to checking a citation than it is to reading prose: does the named id exist as a real resource in this bundle or system; does that resource's own `subject` match the subject of the resource pointing at it; and, when both resources carry dates, does the timing make sense — does the Observation's `effectiveDateTime` actually fall within the Encounter's `period`? A potassium drawn on March 3rd referencing an encounter that ran March 1st to March 2nd has failed that third check even though the first two pass cleanly.

contentSections.question: Put the reference-checking procedure in order.
steps: Look up the referenced resource by its id in the bundle or source system
Confirm the referenced resource actually exists (catches dangling references)
Compare the referenced resource's subject to the referencing resource's subject (catches cross-patient references)
Compare any dates — does the timing fall inside the expected period (catches stale references)
Flag the resource if any step fails, rather than assuming a resolving reference means a correct one
contentSections.explanation: Each step catches a different failure mode, and skipping straight to "does this resolve to something" only catches the dangling case — the cheapest, least dangerous kind of broken reference, because it usually throws an error somewhere downstream on its own. The cross-patient and stale cases resolve cleanly and produce no error anywhere; they're only caught by someone actually comparing subjects and dates.

contentSections.body: A reference that resolves to something is not the same as a reference that resolves to the right something — chasing it means comparing subjects and dates, not just confirming it points at a real id.

title: Reading a v2 message when that's what the system speaks
description: Decoding a pipe-delimited HL7 v2 message — MSH, PID, PV1, OBX segments and the five delimiter characters that give the whole message its grammar — and the escaping failures that make an AI pipeline misparse one.

learningObjectives.text: Decode the segment and field structure of an HL7 v2 message
Diagnose a v2 parsing failure caused by an unescaped delimiter character

contentSections.title: Segments, fields, and the separators that hold it together

contentSections.body: The AI pipeline's lab feed doesn't arrive as JSON. It arrives as this, dumped straight from the interface engine: `MSH|^~\&|LABSYS|RIVERSIDE|CODEPIPE|RIVERSIDE|20260304091500||ORU^R01|MSG00219|P|2.5.1` — and four more segments after it. Reading it means knowing what each of those pipes and carets is doing.

contentSections.problem:
Decode this ORU (observation result) message segment by segment:
`MSH|^~\&|LABSYS|RIVERSIDE|CODEPIPE|RIVERSIDE|20260304091500||ORU^R01|MSG00219|P|2.5.1`
`PID|1||4489^^^RIVERSIDE^MR||OKAFOR^AMARA||19680214|F`
`OBX|1|NM|2160-0^Creatinine^LN||1.4|mg/dL|0.6-1.3|H|||F`

steps.label: Read MSH — the message header and its own delimiter declaration
steps.work: MSH-1 is the field separator itself (`|`). MSH-2 declares the remaining special characters: `^` component separator, `~` repetition separator, `\` escape character, `&` subcomponent separator. MSH-9 (`ORU^R01`) says this is an unsolicited observation result message.
steps.why: Every other segment in the message is parsed using the delimiters MSH declares — get MSH-2 wrong and every downstream field misreads.

steps.label: Read PID — patient identification
steps.work: PID-3 (`4489^^^RIVERSIDE^MR`) is the patient identifier, MR number 4489 at Riverside. PID-5 (`OKAFOR^AMARA`) is family name^given name. PID-7 is date of birth (19680214 = Feb 14, 1968). PID-8 is administrative sex (F).
steps.why: PID-5's caret separates components within one field — family and given name are two components of the same field, not two fields.

steps.label: Read OBX — the observation itself
steps.work: OBX-3 (`2160-0^Creatinine^LN`) is the LOINC code, its display name, and the coding system (LN = LOINC). OBX-5 (`1.4`) is the value. OBX-6 (`mg/dL`) is units. OBX-7 (`0.6-1.3`) is the reference range. OBX-8 (`H`) flags the result as High relative to that range.
steps.why: The abnormal flag in OBX-8 is computed against the specific reference range in OBX-7 — checking the flag without checking the range it was computed against is checking half the story.

blanks.prompt: What test does OBX-3 identify (by LOINC code)?
blanks.why: 4548-4 is the LOINC code for Hemoglobin A1c, given in OBX-3 alongside its display name and coding system.

blanks.prompt: What is the result value and its units?
blanks.why: OBX-5 carries the value (8.9), OBX-6 carries the units (%).

blanks.prompt: Is this result flagged abnormal, and consistent with the reference range shown?
blanks.why: OBX-8 shows H (high), and 8.9% is indeed above the 4.0-5.6% reference range in OBX-7 — the flag and the range agree, which is itself worth checking rather than assuming.

contentSections.procedure: **Read MSH first to get the delimiters → identify each segment by its three-letter code → count fields by pipe, components by caret → cross-check the abnormal flag against the reference range it was computed from.** Skipping straight to the value without reading MSH-2 is how a caret inside a name field gets misread as a field boundary.

contentSections.title: Where an AI mis-parses a v2 message

contentSections.body: A pipeline chokes on a routine ADT feed. The patient's name field arrives as `O'BRIEN^PATRICK^^JR` — and downstream, the patient's suffix ("JR") shows up in a field meant for a middle name, while the actual given name silently drops.

The caret in `O'BRIEN^PATRICK^^JR` is doing its normal job — separating family name, given name, an empty middle-name component, and suffix. Nothing here is malformed. The real failure modes to watch for are subtler: **unescaped delimiter characters inside free text** (a caret or pipe typed literally into a comment field without being escaped using `\S\` for component separator or `\F\` for field separator, which shifts every subsequent field by one); **miscounted repetitions** (`~` separating multiple values in one field, e.g. multiple phone numbers, parsed as if there were only one); and **custom Z-segments** — vendor-specific segments starting with `Z` that carry local extensions a generic parser is built to skip, silently dropping whatever data lived there.

contentSections.scenario: A pipeline processing an ADT (admit/discharge/transfer) message reports the patient's name as "O'BRIEN" with all remaining name components (given name, suffix) missing, even though the source system's chart clearly shows "Patrick O'Brien Jr." was admitted.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely root cause?

options.label: A caret was typed literally somewhere inside a free-text field upstream without being escaped, shifting the parser's field/component boundaries
The patient's given name and suffix were never entered anywhere in the source system
HL7 v2 doesn't support suffixes, so JR is always dropped

feedback.escape: Right. An unescaped delimiter character — most often a caret or pipe typed literally into a free-text field somewhere earlier in the message, without the required escape sequence — shifts every component boundary that follows, and a parser that isn't defending against it silently drops or garbles the fields downstream of the collision.
feedback.missing: The source chart clearly shows the full name — the data exists. The failure is in how it got parsed on the way through, not in whether it was ever recorded.
feedback.spec: HL7 v2's PID-5 field explicitly has a suffix component (the fourth caret-delimited component) — the standard supports it fine. This is a parsing failure, not a spec limitation.

contentSections.mechanism: **A single unescaped delimiter character, typed literally somewhere in a free-text field, is enough to shift every field boundary after it.** This is the same failure family as the classic SQL-injection-adjacent bug: a special character meant to be data gets read as syntax instead, because whatever produced the message didn't escape it. In HL7 v2, the fix is using the declared escape character (`\` by default) with the right escape sequence — `\S\` for a literal component separator, `\F\` for a literal field separator — whenever the delimiter character appears as actual content rather than structure.

contentSections.body: The five characters after MSH-2 aren't decoration — they're the whole message's grammar, and one unescaped delimiter inside free text is enough to shift everything that follows it.

title: Valid, conformant, and still wrong
description: The gap between a coded value being a legal member of its bound value set and being the correct member for this specific case — the axis conformance validation cannot check, and the one this whole track exists to cover.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish value-set membership validity from correctness of the specific value chosen
Identify what a conformance validator did and did not verify about a given resource

contentSections.title: Passing every check that exists

contentSections.body: A patient is admitted overnight for observation after a fall. The AI-assembled Encounter resource passes FHIR conformance validation with zero errors: correct resource type, all required fields present, `class` populated with `AMB` — a real, valid code drawn from HL7's ActEncounterCode value set. `AMB` means ambulatory. This patient was kept overnight.

`AMB` is a legal value. That's exactly the problem: **conformance validation checks whether a code is a member of its bound value set, not whether it's the right member for this case.** The validator confirmed `class` was populated, and that whatever populated it (`AMB`) is a real code HL7 recognizes — it has no mechanism to know this particular encounter was actually an overnight observation stay, which should have been coded `OBSENC`, or possibly `IMP` depending on the organization's admission criteria.

The same gap exists in HL7 v2: PV1-2 (patient class) = `O` for outpatient is a valid code drawn from HL7 table 0004 — and just as wrong, in exactly the same way, for a patient who was actually kept overnight. In both cases, the message is completely standards-conformant. The value inside it is a real code from the right table. And it's the wrong code for what actually happened to this patient.

contentSections.scenario: An Encounter resource for the overnight-observation patient above passes conformance validation with zero errors, `class` coded `AMB`.
contentSections.question: Select every check a standard FHIR conformance validator actually performed on this resource.

items.label: Confirmed resourceType is a real FHIR resource type
Confirmed required fields (like class, status) are present
Confirmed the value in class is a real code from its bound value set (ActEncounterCode)
Confirmed AMB is the clinically/administratively correct class for what actually happened to this patient
Cross-checked the Encounter against the admitting note to see if an overnight stay was documented

explanation.type: Yes — resourceType checking is a base structural requirement of every FHIR resource.
explanation.required: Yes — cardinality rules (which fields are required, 1..1 vs 0..1) are part of what a profile-aware validator checks.
explanation.valueset: Yes — this is exactly what caught nothing here: AMB is genuinely a valid member of the ActEncounterCode value set, so this check passes even though the value is wrong for this case.
explanation.correct: No — nothing about conformance validation reasons about what actually happened clinically. It has no access to — and no mechanism to compare against — the admitting note.
explanation.matches-note: No — conformance validation operates on the resource in isolation against its schema and value-set bindings. It does not read source documentation at all.

contentSections.synthesis: Three real checks happened, and all three passed. None of the three were ever capable of catching that AMB was the wrong choice — that check lives entirely outside conformance validation, in a human comparing the coded value against what the note actually says happened.

contentSections.title: What checking correctness actually requires

contentSections.body: Closing this module: a reviewer's job runs on an axis conformance validation was never built to touch. Every resource in this module's examples — the mismatched reference, the misparsed name, the AMB-coded overnight stay — would pass a validator cleanly. Every one of them required actually reading the source and comparing.

Standards check two things well: shape (is this the right resource type, are required fields present, do references point at existing ids) and vocabulary membership (is this coded value a real member of the terminology it's bound to). Neither check requires understanding the patient in front of you. What you check is a third thing, orthogonal to both: does the *specific* coded value chosen — among all the legal ones available — match what the source documentation actually describes. That's not a smaller version of what conformance validation does; it's a genuinely different question, and it's the one every module after this one keeps coming back to. Module two goes further into exactly this gap for diagnosis coding specifically — codes that individually pass every check and still misdescribe the patient when read together.

contentSections.title: The overnight-observation encounter
contentSections.opening: You're reviewing the Encounter resource above: class = AMB, conformance validation clean, admitting note clearly documents an overnight observation stay after a fall.

n1.situation: The claim is queued for submission with class = AMB. You have the admitting note open beside it, which documents "admit to observation, overnight, reassess in AM."
n1.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Approve as-is — it passed conformance validation, so it's fine
choices.consequence: The claim submits with class AMB. Observation-level utilization and, depending on the payer, reimbursement calculations are now based on an ambulatory encounter that was actually an overnight stay — a discrepancy that surfaces later, at audit, as much harder to explain than it would have been to fix now.

choices.label: Correct class to OBSENC, noting the admitting note's "admit to observation, overnight" as the basis
choices.consequence: The corrected Encounter now matches what the note documents, with a traceable reason recorded.

choices.label: Escalate to ask whether this organization's criteria treat this stay as OBSENC or IMP
choices.consequence: A reasonable move if your organization's admission criteria for observation-vs-inpatient are genuinely ambiguous for this case — but AMB (ambulatory) is wrong under any of those criteria, so at minimum that much can be corrected now rather than escalated.

good.summary: You corrected the class to match documented reality and left a traceable basis for the correction.
good.lesson: AMB passing conformance validation was never evidence it was right — the note settled that question, and once you'd read it, there was nothing left to defer.

mixed.summary: Escalating the OBSENC-vs-IMP distinction is defensible, but AMB itself didn't need to wait for that answer.
mixed.lesson: Not every uncertainty is equally uncertain — separate what's genuinely ambiguous from what the note already settled, and fix the settled part now.

costly.summary: Conformance validation was treated as proof of correctness, and it isn't — the discrepancy surfaces later, at audit, harder to explain than it would have been to catch now.
costly.lesson: "It passed validation" answers a narrower question than "it's correct." Confusing the two is exactly the failure mode this module exists to close.

contentSections.body: Conformant answers the question "is this a legal value." Correct answers a different question entirely: "is this the actual value, for this patient, at this encounter." A reviewer's job lives entirely in that second question.

title: Review a FHIR bundle against the encounter it describes
description: Given a source encounter note and an AI-assembled FHIR bundle claiming to represent it, find every discrepancy — structural, reference, and conformant-but-wrong — and write a review a supervisor could act on.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's checks systematically across an entire bundle rather than one resource at a time
Produce a discrepancy review naming the specific evidence for each finding

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the shape of review you'll actually do: a source note on one side, an AI-assembled bundle claiming to represent it on the other, and the job is finding every place they disagree — not just the obvious ones.

contentSections.title: Review a FHIR bundle against the encounter it describes
contentSections.brief: You're given a source encounter note (an ED visit) and a FHIR bundle an AI pipeline assembled from it, containing Patient, Encounter, Condition, and Observation resources. The bundle passes conformance validation with zero errors. Your job is to find every discrepancy between what the bundle claims and what the note actually documents — resource typing, broken references, and conformant-but-wrong coded values — and write them up as a reviewer would.
contentSections.deliverable: A discrepancy review listing each finding, the specific resource and field involved, what the note actually documents, and what should change — or a clean bill of health for any resource you checked and found correct.

stages.title: Write the source encounter note
stages.instructions: Write a realistic ED encounter note (6-10 sentences: chief complaint, relevant history, exam findings, at least two vitals/labs with values, assessment, disposition).
stages.checkpoint: You have a complete, specific ED note with a chief complaint, at least two measured vitals/labs, a stated diagnosis, and a disposition.

stages.title: Assemble a bundle with seeded issues
stages.instructions: Assemble a FHIR bundle "as an AI pipeline would" from that note — Patient, Encounter, Condition, and at least two Observation resources. Deliberately seed it with at least four discrepancies across these categories: one resource-typing error (a fact placed in the wrong resource type), one broken reference (dangling, cross-patient, or stale — your choice), one conformant-but-wrong coded value (legal code, wrong for this case), and one resource that's actually correct as a control. Keep a private answer key of which is which.
stages.checkpoint: You have a bundle with at least four seeded issues spanning three different categories, plus one deliberately-correct resource, and a private answer key.

stages.title: Review the bundle cold
stages.instructions: Set the answer key aside. Go through the bundle resource by resource: confirm each resource type matches the fact it's carrying, chase every reference (does it resolve, does the subject match, do the dates fit), and for every coded field, compare the specific value chosen against what the note documents — not just whether it's a legal code. Write down every discrepancy you find as you find it, with the specific field and the specific sentence in the note it contradicts.
stages.checkpoint: You've reviewed every resource in the bundle and have a written finding, or a written "checked, no issue," for each one.

stages.title: Self-check against your own answer key
stages.instructions: Compare your findings against the answer key you set aside. Did you catch all four seeded issues? Did you flag anything as a discrepancy that was actually correct? For anything you missed, figure out why — did you skip chasing a reference, or read a value without comparing it to the specific sentence in the note?
stages.checkpoint: You know exactly which seeded issues you caught, which you missed, and can name the specific check that would have caught each miss.

rubric.criterion: Every resource in the bundle was checked, not just the ones that looked suspicious
rubric.meets: The written review shows evidence of a pass over every resource — typing, references, and coded values — not only the ones that turned out to have issues.

rubric.criterion: Each finding names the specific field and the specific sentence in the note it contradicts
rubric.meets: No finding is a generic "this seems off" — each one quotes or closely paraphrases the exact part of the note that the resource disagrees with.

rubric.criterion: Findings span more than one category of error
rubric.meets: The review isn't all one kind of catch — it reflects checking resource typing, reference integrity, and value correctness as three separate passes.

rubric.criterion: At least one resource is confirmed correct with a written reason, not silently skipped
rubric.meets: The review includes a positive confirmation for at least one resource, showing the reviewer actually checked it rather than assuming no news is good news.

rubric.criterion: The self-check pass produced an honest accounting of what was missed and why
rubric.meets: The write-up names any seeded issue that was missed and identifies which specific check — typing, reference-chasing, or value comparison — would have caught it.

contentSections.body: A bundle passing conformance validation is the starting line for a review, not the finish line — the actual work is comparing every resource, every reference, and every coded value against what the source documentation says happened.

title: Checkpoint — HL7 and FHIR in Practice
description: Ungraded retrieval covering this module — what standards guarantee, the four core FHIR resources, reference-chasing, v2 segment reading, and the conformant-versus-correct distinction. This is the first module of the phase, so all ten questions draw from it.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions without support

contentSections.title: Checkpoint
Checkpoint — HL7 and FHIR in Practice
contentSections.framing: Let's see what stuck. This is the first module of this phase, so every question below pulls from it — nothing to space back to yet.

questions.from: This module — Why standards exist
questions.prompt: What does an HL7/FHIR standard actually guarantee about a message?

options.label: Shared syntax and coded-vocabulary bindings — not that the values inside are clinically true
That every value in the message has been clinically verified
That the sending and receiving systems are made by the same vendor

questions.explanation: A standard's guarantee is structural and vocabulary-level: the message can be parsed, and coded fields draw from an agreed terminology. Truth of the specific value is a separate question entirely.

questions.from: This module — FHIR resources
questions.prompt: Which FHIR resource type carries a discrete measured value like a lab result or vital sign, coded to LOINC?

options.label: Observation
Condition
Encounter

questions.explanation: Observation carries measured or reported facts — vitals, labs, exam findings — bound to LOINC. Condition carries diagnoses; Encounter carries the visit itself.

questions.from: This module — References between resources
questions.prompt: A Condition's `encounter` reference resolves to a real Encounter resource whose `subject` names a different patient than the Condition's own `subject`. What kind of failure is this?

options.label: Cross-patient reference
Dangling reference
Not a failure — references only need to resolve to something real

questions.explanation: The reference resolves fine — to a real resource — which is exactly why this is the cross-patient case, not the dangling case. The mismatch is in the subjects, something a base conformance validator doesn't check.

questions.from: This module — References between resources
questions.prompt: Why doesn't a standard FHIR conformance validator catch a cross-patient reference?

options.label: Because subject-matching across referenced resources is a semantic consistency rule, not a structural/syntax requirement the validator checks by default
It's a known bug in most FHIR validators that will eventually be fixed
Validators are structurally unable to read reference fields at all

questions.explanation: Validators absolutely read references — they check that they're well-formed and often that they resolve. What they don't do by default is cross-check that the resolved resource's subject matches the referencing resource's own subject; that's a semantic rule some organizations add, not a base guarantee.

questions.from: This module — Reading a v2 message
questions.prompt: In an HL7 v2 message, what does MSH-2 declare?

options.label: The delimiter characters (component, repetition, escape, subcomponent) used throughout the rest of the message
The patient's identifying information
Only the name of the sending application

questions.explanation: MSH-2 declares the special characters — by default `^~\&` — that every later segment is parsed with. Patient information lives in PID; MSH-3/MSH-4 (not MSH-2) name the sending application/facility.

questions.from: This module — Reading a v2 message
questions.prompt: What's the most likely effect of an unescaped caret typed literally into a v2 free-text field?

options.label: The parser reads it as a component separator, shifting how that field — and potentially later fields — are parsed
The whole message is automatically rejected before parsing
Nothing — free text is exempt from delimiter parsing

questions.explanation: A parser can't distinguish an unescaped literal caret from an intentional component separator — it silently misparses rather than rejecting the message outright, which is exactly why this failure mode is dangerous.

questions.from: This module — Valid, conformant, and still wrong
questions.prompt: An Encounter's `class` field is coded AMB for a patient who was actually admitted overnight for observation. Would a standard conformance validator flag this?

options.label: No — AMB is a legal member of the ActEncounterCode value set, so the field passes validation even though it's the wrong choice for this case
Yes — validators cross-check class against admission length automatically
Only if the encounter lasted more than 24 hours

questions.explanation: AMB is a real, legal code — the validator's vocabulary check passes. Nothing about conformance validation compares the coded class against admission length or documentation; that comparison is a reviewer's job.

questions.from: This module — Valid, conformant, and still wrong
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between "conformant" and "correct" as this module uses the terms?

options.label: Conformant means the value is a legal member of its bound vocabulary; correct means it's the right member for this specific case, checked against source documentation
They mean the same thing — a resource that's conformant is, by definition, correct
Conformant applies only to FHIR; correct applies only to HL7 v2

questions.explanation: This is the module's central distinction: conformance is a narrower, checkable-in-isolation property. Correctness requires comparing the chosen value against the specific patient's documented reality, which no automated validator does.

questions.from: This module — FHIR resources
questions.prompt: A note states "BMI 31.2, calculated." Where does that raw numeric value belong?

options.label: Observation, coded to the appropriate LOINC identifier
Condition, since BMI is a diagnosis
Either resource type works equally well

questions.explanation: A calculated numeric value is a measurement, not a diagnosis — it belongs on Observation. A related Z-code for BMI category could exist as a separate Condition, but the raw value itself is an Observation.

questions.from: This module — References between resources
questions.prompt: What's the correct order of steps for chasing a reference to confirm it's trustworthy?

options.label: Confirm the referenced resource exists → compare subjects → compare dates/period → flag if any step fails
Confirm the referenced resource exists, and stop there — that's sufficient
Compare dates first, since that's the most common failure

questions.explanation: Existence-checking alone only catches dangling references — it has to be followed by a subject comparison (catches cross-patient) and a date/period comparison (catches stale) to cover all three failure modes.
