title: The validator checks shape, not truth
description: A record can pass every automated coding validator — every required field present, every code a real member of its code set, every cardinality rule satisfied — and still misdescribe what happened to the patient. Structural validation and clinical correctness are different, unrelated checks.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a coding/claims validator checks and what it cannot check
Identify a structurally valid record that is clinically wrong

contentSections.title: Zero errors, one wrong patient

contentSections.body: A claim for a 34-year-old male patient runs through the clearinghouse's edit checks before submission: NPI valid, place of service valid, ICD-10-CM code Z34.90 (encounter for supervision of normal pregnancy, unspecified trimester) present and correctly formatted, CPT code for the office visit present, modifier usage clean. Zero edit errors. The claim submits. Z34.90 is also, structurally, nothing but a well-formed code — nothing about the edit engine noticed, or was built to notice, that it was attached to a male patient.

Module one covered this gap for HL7/FHIR resources — a coded value can be a legal member of its value set and still be the wrong member for this patient. This module covers the same gap from a different angle: **claims and coding validators** — the software that runs before a claim submits, whether built into the EHR, the clearinghouse, or a standalone scrubber — check things like: is every required field populated, is each code a real, currently-valid code in its code set (not a deleted or outdated ICD-10-CM code), do modifiers pair correctly with the procedures they modify, does the diagnosis code support medical necessity for the procedure billed under this payer's published edits.

Every one of those checks can pass on a claim that misdescribes the patient. A pregnancy-supervision code on a male patient's chart would, in practice, usually also fail a payer's sex-edit — but plenty of clinically impossible or contradictory combinations exist that no payer edit catches, because the edit rules are built around known, common error patterns, not around exhaustively verifying every clinical fact against every other one.

contentSections.scenario:
Two claims are queued for submission on the same afternoon.

**Claim A:** ICD-10-CM S52.501A (unspecified fracture of the lower end of the right radius, initial encounter), CPT 25605 (closed treatment of distal radial fracture, with manipulation) — both codes present, correctly formatted, modifiers clean.

**Claim B:** the same two codes, but the source note documents a fracture of the *left* wrist, splinted without manipulation.
contentSections.question: Which claim would a standard claims-edit validator flag before submission?

options.label: Claim B — the validator cross-checks laterality and manipulation status against the source note
Neither — both claims are structurally well-formed, and a standard edit engine has no access to the source note to compare against
Both — mismatched laterality always trips a hard edit

feedback.b: A validator checking claim structure has no access to the source clinical note at all — it can't compare a code against documentation it never sees. Laterality mismatches like this one are exactly the kind of error that requires a human reading both the code and the note.
feedback.neither: Right. Both claims are structurally identical — same codes, same formatting, same clean modifier pairing. A claims-edit engine operates on the claim's own fields and payer-specific business rules; it has no channel back to the source documentation to notice that Claim B's codes describe the wrong side and the wrong treatment. This is invisible to automated validation by construction, not by an oversight someone could patch.
feedback.both: There's no universal hard edit for laterality mismatch against a note the edit engine never reads — some payers flag specific known-risky combinations, but a generic wrong-side error like this one typically sails through unless a human catches it.

contentSections.concept: **A claims validator checks the claim against itself and against payer rules — never against the clinical note that generated it.** That's the whole reason a human reviewer sits between the coder (human or AI) and submission: the validator's blind spot is exactly the reviewer's job.

contentSections.title: What "passed validation" is actually a claim about

contentSections.body: A biller says, of a denied claim that had passed every pre-submission edit: "I don't understand, it was clean." It was clean — clean is a real, narrower claim than "correct," and the payer's post-submission medical-necessity review checks a layer the pre-submission edit engine never touched.

It's worth being precise about what "passed validation" is actually asserting, because the phrase gets used loosely in a way that quietly expands its meaning. A clean pre-submission edit check asserts: required fields are populated, codes are real and current, formatting rules are met, and known payer-specific combination rules (this diagnosis supports this procedure, this modifier is allowed with this code) aren't violated. It does not assert: the codes match the documentation, the codes are internally consistent with each other beyond the specific combinations the payer bothered to write a rule for, or the sequence of diagnoses reflects what was actually addressed at this visit. A record that's clean by every one of those checks can still misdescribe the encounter in ways this module spends its remaining four lessons on: wrong laterality, contradictory codes, wrong principal diagnosis, and internally-consistent-but-clinically-impossible combinations.

contentSections.code:
Denial letter excerpt, three weeks after a "clean" claim submitted:

"Claim denied. CPT 29881 (arthroscopy, knee, with
meniscectomy) billed with ICD-10-CM M25.561 (pain in
right knee, unspecified) as sole supporting diagnosis.
Pain alone does not establish medical necessity for a
meniscectomy without a corresponding meniscal tear
diagnosis (e.g. S83.2- series) documented."
contentSections.question: What does this denial reveal about what "the claim was clean" actually meant at submission?

options.label: It reveals the pre-submission edit check was buggy and should have caught this

It reveals that "clean" meant the claim was structurally well-formed and passed the payer's automated combination rules that existed at submission time — not that a human had confirmed the diagnosis actually supported the procedure clinically
It reveals nothing new — this denial is unrelated to whether the claim was clean

feedback.buggy: The edit engine did exactly what it's built to do — check known rule combinations. Whether "pain, unspecified" alone supports a meniscectomy without a tear diagnosis is a medical-necessity judgment call some payers' automated edits don't encode as a hard rule, especially if the specific combination wasn't one their rule library covers; that's a gap in rule coverage, not a malfunction.
feedback.meaning: Right. "Clean" described the claim's structural and known-rule compliance at the moment it left the building — a real, narrower fact than "a human confirmed this diagnosis clinically justifies this procedure." The denial shows exactly where that narrower guarantee ran out.
feedback.unrelated: It's directly related — the denial is the downstream cost of treating "passed pre-submission validation" as equivalent to "medically justified," which is precisely the gap this lesson is naming.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the pattern worth internalizing early in this module: a denial that arrives *after* a clean submission isn't proof the validator failed — it's proof the validator was never checking the thing that ultimately mattered. Reading the specific denial reason back against what the pre-submission edit actually verifies is how you tell the difference between a system bug and a genuine limit of what automated validation covers.

contentSections.body: "Passed validation" is a real but narrow claim: the codes are current, well-formatted, and don't violate a known payer rule. It says nothing about whether the codes match the note — that check is yours.

title: Right code, wrong laterality, wrong encounter
description: Three ways a code can be exactly the right family and completely wrong in the specific detail that matters: the wrong side, the wrong extension, or attached to the wrong visit entirely.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a laterality mismatch between a code and its source documentation
Identify a code correctly chosen for the wrong encounter

contentSections.title: The right family, the wrong side

contentSections.body: Op note: "Left knee arthroscopy with partial medial meniscectomy." Proposed code: M23.201 (derangement of meniscus due to old tear or injury, right knee). The diagnosis family is exactly right — a meniscal derangement code for a meniscectomy. The side is backwards.

ICD-10-CM builds laterality directly into thousands of codes — musculoskeletal, ophthalmologic, and many others carry separate codes for right, left, and (for some categories) bilateral or unspecified. That specificity exists precisely so laterality errors are catchable *if someone checks the code against the side actually documented* — it's not caught automatically by the code being real, current, and correctly formatted. A right-side code and a left-side code from the same family are equally valid, equally current, equally well-formatted members of ICD-10-CM. Only one of them matches this note.

The same failure shows up in reverse: coding to "unspecified" laterality (M23.209, derangement of meniscus, unspecified knee) when the note clearly documents a side. Coding guidance is explicit that you code to the highest level of specificity the documentation supports — defaulting to unspecified when a side is actually stated isn't a safe, conservative choice, it's underspecifying a fact the record already contains.

contentSections.scenario: An AI coding pipeline proposes M23.201 (right knee) for the left-knee arthroscopy note above, with a confidence score of 0.86 — high confidence, not a borderline call.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely mechanism behind a high-confidence laterality error like this?

options.label: The pipeline correctly identified "meniscectomy" and the general code family from strong textual cues, but pattern-matched the laterality from a less reliable signal — a mention of the right knee elsewhere in the patient's history, or simply the more common coding pattern in its training data — rather than from the operative side stated in this note
ICD-10-CM doesn't actually have separate codes for right and left knee, so any laterality choice is equally arbitrary
High confidence scores are never wrong; this must be a coincidental typo in how the case was presented

feedback.wrongsignal: Right. Confidence, as covered in the foundations track, measures how strongly the model's overall pattern matched something in its training — it doesn't verify which specific detail (like laterality) the match was actually keyed on. A model can be very confident about the diagnosis family while quietly pulling the laterality from the wrong sentence, or from a more common pattern, rather than from the specific side this note documents.
feedback.nocodes: ICD-10-CM's musculoskeletal chapter is built specifically around laterality-specific codes — M23.201 (right) and M23.202 (left) are both real, distinct, current codes. The codes exist; the pipeline picked the wrong one.
feedback.impossible: High confidence is a measure of pattern strength, not a guarantee of correctness on every specific field the code encodes — a model can be genuinely confident about the wrong laterality if it latched onto the wrong signal in the note.

contentSections.mechanism: **A high confidence score reflects how strongly the overall pattern matched, not that every individual detail inside the matched code was independently verified.** Laterality is exactly the kind of detail that can get pulled from the wrong sentence — an earlier visit, a different joint mentioned in passing, or simply the statistically more common side in similar cases — while the rest of the code family is genuinely, confidently correct.

contentSections.title: The right code, the wrong visit

contentSections.body: A patient has two encounters eleven days apart: an ED visit for a fall, and a follow-up primary-care visit for an unrelated annual physical. An AI pipeline processing the follow-up visit's claim attaches S72.001A (unspecified fracture of the right femur, initial encounter) — a real diagnosis this patient genuinely has, correctly coded, correctly formatted, attached to the wrong encounter.

This failure mode doesn't require the code to be wrong at all — S72.001A may be exactly right for what happened to this patient. What's wrong is which encounter it's attached to. A pipeline reconciling a patient's full problem list against each new claim can pull forward an existing, active diagnosis onto a visit that never actually addressed it — the same copy-forward risk covered for documentation in the foundations track, showing up here on the coding side instead. Encounter-based coding requires the condition to be genuinely relevant to *this specific visit's* medical decision-making, evaluation, or treatment — not simply present somewhere on the patient's active problem list. A fracture from eleven days ago that wasn't examined, discussed, or treated at today's unrelated physical shouldn't ride along onto today's claim just because it's still technically active.

contentSections.question: If the follow-up visit's note briefly mentions "patient also reports fracture healing as expected" in the review-of-systems, in one sentence, does that one mention change whether S72.001A should be coded on today's claim?
contentSections.answer: It's a closer call, but a single passing mention in review-of-systems, with no exam, evaluation, or treatment decision devoted to it, is thinner support than an actual assessment-and-plan entry — many organizations' coding guidance would still say this doesn't rise to "addressed" in the sense that justifies coding it, though a genuinely borderline case like this is a reasonable one to flag for a second opinion rather than decide unilaterally either way.
contentSections.hint: Compare "mentioned in passing" to "evaluated, discussed, or factored into a decision" — where does one sentence in review-of-systems fall?

contentSections.body: A code can be the exact right diagnosis for this patient and still be wrong on the claim — because it's the wrong side, or because it's attached to a visit that never actually addressed it.

title: Codes that contradict each other in one record
description: A record where every individual code is valid, but two or more codes together describe something that can't simultaneously be true — resolved and active at once, or a treatment that presupposes a diagnosis the record never actually assigns.

learningObjectives.text: Identify two codes within one record that contradict each other
Explain why a validator that checks each code individually misses cross-code contradictions

contentSections.title: Individually fine, together impossible

contentSections.body: One encounter's code list: Z87.891 (personal history of nicotine dependence — meaning *former* smoker, resolved), and, three lines later, F17.210 (nicotine dependence, cigarettes, uncomplicated — meaning *current, active* dependence). Both codes are real. Both are correctly formatted. Read on their own, in isolation, neither one is wrong. Read together, they assert the patient both used to smoke and currently smokes as an active dependence, in the same breath.

A validator checking each code line by line — is this a real code, is it current, is it formatted correctly — has no reason to flag either Z87.891 or F17.210. Each passes every single-code check cleanly. The contradiction only exists in the *relationship* between the two, and finding it requires holding both codes in mind at once and asking whether they can both be true of the same patient at the same encounter.

This is a genuinely different skill from the laterality and wrong-encounter checks in the last lesson, which compare one code against the source note. Here, you're comparing a code against *another code on the same record* — and it's worth building a habit of reading a record's full code list together, not one code at a time, specifically to catch this.

contentSections.scenario: A patient's encounter carries this code list: I10 (essential hypertension), E78.5 (hyperlipidemia, unspecified), Z00.00 (encounter for general adult medical exam without abnormal findings).
contentSections.question: Select every pair of codes in this list, if any, that contradicts another code in the same list.

items.label: I10 and E78.5 together
Z00.00 ("without abnormal findings") alongside two active chronic diagnoses (I10, E78.5) coded at the same visit
I10 alone contradicts E78.5 alone

explanation.htn-lipid: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia are two entirely separate, commonly co-occurring conditions — nothing about coding both at once is contradictory.
explanation.z00-with-findings: Right. Z00.00 specifically means "without abnormal findings." Coding it at the same encounter as two active chronic disease diagnoses is asserting, in the same code list, both that nothing abnormal was found and that two abnormal chronic conditions were addressed. The correct wellness code for a visit where chronic conditions ARE addressed is Z00.01 (with abnormal findings) — a one-digit difference in the code that changes what the whole visit is asserting.
explanation.i10-e78: Neither code makes a claim about the other in isolation — the contradiction, where one exists, is specifically about Z00.00's own "without abnormal findings" language conflicting with what else is on the list, not about I10 and E78.5 conflicting with each other.

contentSections.synthesis: The contradiction here isn't between two diagnosis codes — it's between an encounter-type code that explicitly claims a negative finding and two diagnosis codes on the same list that are, definitionally, findings. Catching it means reading the encounter code's actual definition, not just treating it as a formality.

contentSections.title: A procedure that presupposes a diagnosis the record never assigns

contentSections.body: A claim lists CPT 47562 (laparoscopic cholecystectomy) and, as the sole diagnosis code, K59.00 (constipation, unspecified). No gallbladder-related diagnosis — no cholelithiasis (K80.-), no cholecystitis (K81.-) — appears anywhere on the record.

This is the same family of contradiction as the Z00.00 example, wearing a different shape: a procedure code that, by its nature, presupposes a specific kind of diagnosis (you don't remove a gallbladder for constipation), paired with a diagnosis code that has nothing to do with the procedure performed. Each code individually is completely valid — 47562 is a real procedure code, K59.00 is a real diagnosis code — and a validator checking each in isolation has no complaint about either.

The contradiction surfaces only when you ask the question a payer's medical-necessity reviewer eventually will: does *this* diagnosis code plausibly justify *this* procedure. A gallbladder procedure needs a gallbladder-relevant diagnosis on the claim; constipation alone doesn't supply one, whether or not the patient's actual chart, somewhere, documents the real reason (which this coding scenario suggests may simply be missing from the claim, not necessarily missing from the encounter — a distinction worth flagging back to whoever's assembling the claim rather than guessing which gallbladder code to insert).

contentSections.question: If you're reviewing this claim and the source note does, in fact, document acute cholecystitis with imaging-confirmed gallstones, what should you do — silently add K81.0 (acute cholecystitis) yourself, or flag it?
contentSections.answer: Correct the code — this isn't a genuine ambiguity, it's a clear omission you can resolve from documentation that already exists. Add the diagnosis the note actually supports (here, likely K80.- or K81.- depending on what's documented) and note the basis. Escalating this as if it were ambiguous would be treating a fixable gap as if it required someone else's judgment when the note already settles it.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to a genuinely ambiguous case versus one where the note plainly states the answer and it just didn't make it onto the claim.

contentSections.body: Some contradictions live between two codes on the same record, not inside either code alone — which means catching them requires reading the whole code list together, not checking each line in isolation.

title: Sequencing: which diagnosis is principal and why it matters
description: When a visit has multiple diagnoses, the order they're listed in isn't cosmetic — the principal diagnosis carries specific coding-guideline meaning, and getting it wrong changes reimbursement and severity classification even when every individual code is correct.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what makes a diagnosis 'principal' under coding guidelines
Identify a case where the wrong diagnosis was sequenced as principal

contentSections.title: The list has an order for a reason

contentSections.body: An inpatient stay: a patient is admitted primarily for management of a diabetic foot ulcer requiring IV antibiotics and wound debridement, and incidentally has well-controlled hypertension noted and continued on home medication with no active management needed. The claim lists I10 (hypertension) first, the foot ulcer diagnosis second.

For an inpatient stay, coding guidelines define the **principal diagnosis** as the condition, after study, chiefly responsible for occasioning the admission — not necessarily the most severe condition present, and not simply whichever diagnosis a coder or pipeline lists first out of habit. Sequencing isn't a formatting preference; it's a coded assertion about *why this admission happened*, and it feeds directly into DRG (diagnosis-related group) assignment for inpatient reimbursement, severity-of-illness classification, and quality/outcome reporting tied to that specific admission reason.

In the example above, the foot ulcer — the actual reason this patient was admitted, requiring IV antibiotics and debridement — should be sequenced as principal. The well-controlled hypertension, addressed only by continuing an existing medication with no new management, is a secondary diagnosis: real, correctly coded, appropriately documented, and in the wrong position on the list. Every code is individually valid. The sequence tells the wrong story about why the patient was admitted.

contentSections.problem: Inpatient admission note: "Patient admitted for acute exacerbation of COPD with hypoxia, started on IV steroids and nebulizer treatments, oxygen supplementation required. History of well-controlled GERD, continued on home omeprazole, not otherwise addressed." Proposed sequencing: E876 GERD listed as principal, COPD exacerbation listed as secondary. Determine the correct sequencing.

steps.label: Identify what actually occasioned the admission
steps.work: The note states the reason for admission directly: acute COPD exacerbation with hypoxia, requiring IV steroids, nebulizers, and supplemental oxygen — active, escalating treatment.
steps.why: "Chiefly responsible for occasioning the admission" is asking exactly this question: what would have caused this patient to be admitted today, if nothing else on their problem list existed?

steps.label: Identify what was merely continued, not actively managed
steps.work: GERD is mentioned only as history, continued on an existing home medication, with no escalation, no new workup, no active decision-making devoted to it during this stay.
steps.why: A condition present and continued on autopilot is real and codable as a secondary diagnosis, but it didn't occasion anything — the patient wasn't admitted because of their GERD.

steps.label: Re-sequence
steps.work: COPD exacerbation with hypoxia (the appropriate ICD-10-CM code from the J44.1- series) becomes principal. GERD (K21.9) is sequenced as a secondary diagnosis.
steps.why: This sequencing now matches both coding guidelines and the clinical narrative the note itself tells — the two should always agree, and when they don't, the sequencing is what needs to change, not the note.

faded.problem: Inpatient note: "Admitted for community-acquired pneumonia requiring IV antibiotics and continuous pulse oximetry monitoring. Type 2 diabetes, stable, home metformin continued without adjustment." Proposed: E11.9 (T2DM) principal, pneumonia secondary.

blanks.why: The note directly names pneumonia, requiring active IV treatment and monitoring, as the reason for admission.

blanks.prompt: Was the diabetes actively managed or merely continued?
blanks.why: "Stable" and "continued without adjustment" is the same signature as the GERD example — present, real, but not what drove today's admission.

blanks.prompt: What should the correct principal diagnosis be?
blanks.why: Pneumonia should be sequenced first, as principal; T2DM sequenced as a secondary diagnosis, same correction pattern as the worked example.

contentSections.procedure: **Ask what would have caused this admission if nothing else on the problem list existed → distinguish actively-managed from merely-continued → sequence the actively-managed, admission-driving condition as principal.** A condition being more severe, more chronic, or listed first out of habit doesn't override what the note itself says actually happened.

contentSections.title: Why this changes more than the order on a page

contentSections.body: Two inpatient claims, identical diagnosis codes, opposite sequencing: one lists the COPD exacerbation as principal, the other lists the incidental hypertension as principal. Same codes. Different DRG. Different reimbursement. Different severity classification attached to this admission in the hospital's own quality data.

This is what makes sequencing a genuine error category rather than a stylistic one: every code on both claims could be individually valid and current, a validator would flag neither claim, and the two claims would still produce materially different downstream numbers — reimbursement calculated against the wrong DRG, severity-of-illness scoring that misrepresents how sick this admission actually was, and quality/outcome metrics attributed to the wrong condition. An AI pipeline that gets the diagnosis-and-code selection right but the *order* wrong has produced a claim that's wrong in a way that's structurally invisible and financially real.

contentSections.scenario: A hospital audits 200 inpatient claims from an AI-assisted coding pipeline and finds a small but consistent share where the principal diagnosis was sequenced incorrectly — a real secondary condition placed first instead of the condition that actually drove the admission — even though every individual code on those claims was valid and current.
contentSections.question: For illustration: if even a modest 3% of claims in a large hospital's inpatient volume carry a sequencing error like this, and a sequencing error shifts DRG-based reimbursement by a few hundred dollars on average per claim, roughly how many claims would that be at a hospital discharging 15,000 inpatients a year?
contentSections.explanation: 3% of 15,000 is 450 claims a year — illustrative arithmetic, not a real audited figure, but the shape of it is the point: a per-claim error rate that sounds small compounds into a real number of claims, and because each one is individually valid-looking, none of them get caught by a validator built to check codes rather than sequencing logic. This is exactly why sequencing deserves its own dedicated check rather than being assumed to ride along with correct code selection.

contentSections.body: Sequencing is a coded assertion about why the admission happened, not a formatting choice — the principal diagnosis is whatever the note says actually occasioned the stay, and getting it backwards changes reimbursement and severity data even when every code is individually correct.

title: Records that are internally consistent and clinically impossible
description: Closing the module: records where nothing contradicts anything else on the list, every code matches its own definition, and the whole record still describes something that couldn't have actually happened — because the gap is between the record and clinical reality, not between one part of the record and another.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a record that is internally consistent but clinically implausible given the timeline or physiology
Distinguish internal contradiction (lesson 3) from clinical implausibility (this lesson)

contentSections.title: Nothing on the list disagrees with anything else

contentSections.body: A record: encounter dated March 3rd, Condition O80 (encounter for full-term uncomplicated delivery) with onsetDateTime March 3rd, and a second Condition, Z39.2 (routine postpartum follow-up), with an onsetDateTime of March 4th — one day later. Every code is real. Nothing on the list contradicts anything else on the list the way lesson three's examples did. A postpartum follow-up visit scheduled for the day immediately after delivery, before the patient has even been discharged, is not how postpartum care timelines actually work.

Lesson three's contradictions lived *between* two codes reading against each other's own definitions — Z00.00 versus active chronic diagnoses, resolved versus active nicotine dependence. This lesson's failure is different in kind: nothing on the list is definitionally incompatible with anything else. The problem is that the record, taken as a whole, describes a sequence or combination of events that clinical or physiological reality doesn't actually permit — a routine postpartum follow-up encounter typically happens at roughly six weeks, not one day, and while an early postpartum check for a specific complication is real and codable, *routine* follow-up coded for the day after delivery describes a timeline that doesn't correspond to how that specific service is actually delivered.

Catching this requires a different kind of knowledge than catching an internal contradiction: not "do these two codes' own definitions conflict," but "does this combination, given real-world clinical timelines and physiology, actually happen this way." That's closer to the kind of general clinical-plausibility judgment a reviewer builds over time than something checkable purely from code definitions.

contentSections.scenario: A record: Condition Z3A.42 (42 weeks gestation of pregnancy) with an onsetDateTime, and, six days later at a separate encounter, Observation for a newborn's first well-child visit referencing this same mother's chart as the newborn's own record — with the newborn's recorded birthDate matching the mother's Z3A.42 onset date, six days prior.
contentSections.question: Is there a problem here, and if so, which kind?

options.label: No problem — a newborn can be seen for a first well-child visit within a week of birth, and 42 weeks gestation is a real, valid finding
A definitional contradiction — Z3A.42 and a well-child visit can never coexist on related records
The timeline itself is plausible as described — a birth six days before a first well-child visit and a 42-week gestation are each individually unremarkable and consistent with each other

feedback.none: Careful — the question isn't whether either fact is individually fine (they are), it's whether you can spot that in this particular case, unlike the postpartum example, there's actually nothing implausible about the sequence at all.
feedback.contradiction: There's no definitional conflict here the way there was between Z00.00 and active chronic diagnoses in lesson three — 42 weeks gestation and a six-day-old newborn's first well-child visit don't contradict each other's definitions in any way.
feedback.plausible: Right — and naming this explicitly matters as much as catching the postpartum example did: a first well-child visit within the first week or two of life is standard, routine care, and 42 weeks gestation (post-term but within normal clinical range) doesn't conflict with it. Not every combination that looks superficially similar to a red-flag example is actually a problem — treating every timeline as suspect by default is its own failure mode, just as costly as missing a real one.

contentSections.concept: **Clinical-plausibility judgment cuts both ways.** The skill isn't "be suspicious of every timeline" — it's building enough real clinical-workflow knowledge to tell an implausible sequence (postpartum follow-up the day after delivery) from a perfectly ordinary one (a newborn seen within the first week of life) that just happens to involve dates close together.

contentSections.title: Closing the module: three different gaps, one structural blind spot

contentSections.body: This module has walked through three genuinely different ways a record can pass structural validation and still be wrong: a code that doesn't match its own source documentation (lesson two — wrong laterality, wrong encounter), two codes that contradict each other's own definitions (lesson three), and a whole record that's internally consistent but describes a timeline or combination reality doesn't actually produce (this lesson). All three share the same structural blind spot as module one's conformant-but-wrong FHIR values: a validator checking fields, formats, and known rule combinations has no channel back to either the source note or to general clinical-plausibility judgment. That channel is you, in three distinct forms depending on which of these three failure shapes you're looking at.

contentSections.question: Put these three checks in a sensible reading order when reviewing an unfamiliar record — cheapest/most-mechanical first, most judgment-dependent last.
steps: Check each code individually against the source note (right laterality, right encounter, right specificity)
Check the code list against itself for definitional contradictions (resolved-vs-active, findings-code-vs-active-diagnoses)
Check the record as a whole against real-world clinical timelines and physiology for plausibility
contentSections.explanation: This isn't a rigid rule, but it's a useful default order: comparing a code to its own source note is the most mechanical and fastest check, comparing codes to each other requires holding the whole list in mind, and judging plausibility against general clinical-workflow knowledge is the most judgment-dependent and typically the slowest. Doing them in this order means you've caught the cheaper, more obvious errors before spending the most effortful check on a record that might not have needed it.

contentSections.body: A record can fail structural validation in three different ways that all look identical to a validator: wrong against the source, wrong against itself, or wrong against how clinical events actually unfold — and telling them apart is what the rest of this track keeps training.

Distinguish a genuine record-level error from a plausible combination that only looks suspicious

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across three — nothing here expires or times out.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Review a batch that passed validation for clinical sense
description: Given ten records that all cleared automated claims validation, find every one that's actually wrong — laterality/encounter mismatch, cross-code contradiction, sequencing error, or clinical implausibility — and produce a findings list a supervisor could act on.

learningObjectives.text: Apply all four of the module's failure-mode checks systematically across a batch of records
Produce a findings list stating the specific clinical reason each flagged record is wrong

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Ten records, all clean at the validator. Some of them are actually fine. Finding out which is which, and being able to say specifically why, is the whole job this module has been building toward.

contentSections.title: Review a batch that passed validation for clinical sense
contentSections.brief: You're given a source note and a coded record for ten encounters, all of which cleared automated claims validation with zero errors. Some records are genuinely correct. Others contain one of this module's four failure types: wrong laterality/encounter, cross-code contradiction, sequencing error, or clinical implausibility. Review the batch and produce a findings list.
contentSections.deliverable: A findings list covering all ten records: for each, either 'clean, no issue, because ___' or a specific finding naming the failure category, the exact codes/fields involved, and the clinical reasoning that makes it wrong.

stages.title: Build the ten-record batch
stages.instructions: Write ten short encounter notes with their proposed coded records (2-5 codes each). Seed at least six of the ten with exactly one error apiece, spanning all four failure categories from this module (aim for at least one of each category, plus at least one genuinely clean record and one record you find realistically tricky to call). Keep a private answer key.
stages.checkpoint: You have ten records, at least six seeded with a single clear error each across all four categories, at least one clean control, and a private answer key.

stages.title: Pass 1 and 2: note-comparison and cross-code check
stages.instructions: Set the answer key aside. First pass: compare each code against its own source note for laterality, encounter, and specificity mismatches. Second pass: read each record's full code list against itself for definitional contradictions and sequencing errors. Note findings as you go.
stages.checkpoint: Every record has been checked against its source note and against its own code list, with findings recorded for both passes.

stages.title: Pass 3: clinical plausibility
stages.instructions: Third pass: judge each record as a whole against real-world clinical timelines and physiology, independent of the first two passes. Write a finding — or a clean bill — for every record.
stages.checkpoint: All ten records have a final finding or clean-bill statement reflecting all three passes.

stages.title: Self-check against your answer key
stages.instructions: Compare against your answer key. Which seeded errors did you catch? Which did you miss, and which of the three passes would have caught it? Did you flag anything as an error that was actually clean?
stages.checkpoint: You can name, for every miss, which specific pass (note-comparison, cross-code, or plausibility) would have caught it, and you've corrected any false flags on genuinely clean records.

rubric.criterion: All ten records received a genuine review, not just the ones that looked obviously wrong
rubric.meets: The findings list shows evidence of all three passes applied to every record, including the ones ultimately called clean.

rubric.criterion: Findings span more than one of the module's four failure categories
rubric.meets: The write-up isn't all one failure type — it reflects catching laterality/encounter, cross-code, sequencing, and plausibility issues as genuinely distinct checks.

rubric.criterion: Each finding names the specific codes and the specific clinical reasoning, not a generic flag
rubric.meets: No finding reads as 'this looks off' — each one names the exact codes involved and explains, in clinical terms, why the combination or choice is wrong.

rubric.criterion: At least one record is confirmed clean with a stated reason
rubric.meets: The findings list includes a genuine 'no issue, because ___' for at least one record, showing the reviewer didn't default to suspicion.

rubric.criterion: The self-check identifies which specific pass would have caught each miss
rubric.meets: For any seeded error missed, the write-up names which of the three passes (note-comparison, cross-code, plausibility) should have caught it.

contentSections.body: A batch that's clean at the validator is the floor, not the ceiling — three passes (against the note, against itself, against clinical reality) is what actually separates the genuinely correct records from the ones that only look correct.

title: Checkpoint — Structurally Complete, Clinically Wrong
description: Ungraded retrieval — five questions from this module, five spaced back to module one (HL7 and FHIR in Practice). This is the second module of the phase, so there's not yet a third slice to pull from further back.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, with one module of spacing

contentSections.title: Checkpoint
Checkpoint — Structurally Complete, Clinically Wrong
contentSections.framing: Let's see what stuck — half from this module, half spaced back to last module. Nothing further back exists yet.

questions.from: This module — The validator checks shape, not truth
questions.prompt: What does a claims-edit engine's "zero errors" result actually verify?

options.label: Structural well-formedness and compliance with known payer combination rules — not that the codes match the source note
That a human has confirmed medical necessity
That the claim will definitely be paid

questions.explanation: A claims-edit engine checks its own narrower set of rules — structure, formatting, and known combination rules. It has no access to the source note and no ability to guarantee payment, which is a separate, later, payer-side decision.

questions.from: This module — Right code, wrong laterality, wrong encounter
questions.prompt: A patient's active problem list includes a real, correctly-coded condition, but today's visit never addressed it. Should it be coded on today's claim?

options.label: No — encounter-based coding requires the condition to actually be addressed at this specific visit
Yes — any active condition on the problem list should be coded at every visit
Only if the condition is chronic

questions.explanation: Being on the active problem list isn't sufficient — the condition has to have actually been evaluated, monitored, or treated at this visit. Chronic status doesn't change that requirement.

questions.from: This module — Codes that contradict each other
questions.prompt: Why does a per-code validity check typically miss a contradiction between two codes on the same record?

options.label: Because each code passes its own individual checks; the contradiction only exists in comparing the two codes' definitions to each other
Because contradictory codes are always structurally invalid on their own
Because payers never write edits for any code combination

questions.explanation: Both codes in a contradictory pair are typically individually valid — the contradiction lives in the relationship between their definitions, which a per-code check doesn't compare.

questions.from: This module — Sequencing
questions.prompt: What determines which diagnosis is sequenced as principal on an inpatient claim?

options.label: The condition, after study, chiefly responsible for occasioning the admission
Whichever condition is generally most severe
Whichever condition was documented first in the note

questions.explanation: Sequencing follows what actually drove the admission, not general severity or documentation order — a chronic, severe condition merely continued during the stay isn't principal if it didn't occasion the admission.

questions.from: This module — Records that are internally consistent and clinically impossible
questions.prompt: What distinguishes a "clinically implausible" record from an "internally contradictory" one?

options.label: Implausibility requires comparing the whole record against real-world clinical timelines/physiology; contradiction requires comparing two codes' own definitions against each other
They're the same failure mode with different names
Implausibility only applies to obstetric records

questions.explanation: Contradiction is a conflict between two codes' own stated definitions. Implausibility has no such definitional conflict — the problem is the whole record against outside clinical knowledge, and it applies across every specialty, not just obstetrics.

questions.from: Previous module — HL7 and FHIR in Practice
questions.prompt: What does an HL7/FHIR standard actually guarantee about a message?

options.label: Shared syntax and coded-vocabulary bindings — not that the values inside are clinically true
That every value has been clinically verified
That sender and receiver use the same vendor

questions.explanation: Same core distinction as this module, one level down in the stack: a standard guarantees structure and vocabulary membership, not clinical truth.

questions.from: Previous module — HL7 and FHIR in Practice
questions.prompt: A Condition's `encounter` reference resolves to a real Encounter belonging to a different patient than the Condition's own subject. What's this failure called?

options.label: Cross-patient reference
Dangling reference
Stale reference

questions.explanation: It resolves to something real, which rules out dangling — the mismatch is in the subjects, which is specifically the cross-patient failure mode.

questions.from: Previous module — HL7 and FHIR in Practice
questions.prompt: An Encounter's `class` field is coded AMB for a patient who was actually admitted overnight for observation. Would a standard FHIR conformance validator catch this?

options.label: No — AMB is a legal value-set member, so it passes vocabulary validation even though it's the wrong choice
Yes, automatically
Only for stays longer than 48 hours

questions.explanation: AMB is a real code in the bound value set — validation passes. Nothing about conformance checking compares the coded class against actual admission length or documentation.

questions.from: Previous module — HL7 and FHIR in Practice
questions.prompt: What's the difference between "conformant" and "correct" as used in the standards-validation phase so far?

options.label: Conformant means a legal member of the bound vocabulary; correct means the right member for this specific case, checked against source documentation
They're interchangeable terms
Conformant applies only to diagnosis codes, correct only to procedure codes

questions.explanation: This distinction is the throughline connecting both modules so far: a value can be a legal, real code and still be the wrong one for this specific patient or encounter.

questions.from: Previous module — HL7 and FHIR in Practice
questions.prompt: In an HL7 v2 message, what's the effect of a literal, unescaped caret typed into a free-text field?

options.label: The parser reads it as a component separator, potentially shifting how that and later fields are parsed
The message is automatically rejected before parsing
Nothing — free text fields ignore delimiter characters

questions.explanation: An unescaped delimiter character inside text is indistinguishable to a parser from an intentional structural delimiter, which is exactly what makes this failure mode dangerous rather than loud.
