title: Mapping is lossy, and the loss is where harm hides
description: Why translating a clinical concept from one terminology into another (SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM, ICD-9 to ICD-10) is rarely a clean substitution — and why the specific information a mapping drops is exactly the information most likely to matter clinically.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why cross-terminology mapping is inherently lossy rather than a simple lookup
Identify a case where a mapping's loss changed something clinically meaningful

contentSections.title: Two vocabularies, built for different jobs

contentSections.body: A clinician documents a diagnosis in SNOMED CT — the terminology most EHR problem lists actually run on — as concept 8186001, "peripheral neuropathy due to type 2 diabetes mellitus." For billing, that has to become an ICD-10-CM code. The National Library of Medicine's SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM map is the standard bridge for exactly this translation. It correctly lands on E11.42 here. It doesn't always land this cleanly — and this module is about the specific, predictable shapes of when it doesn't.

SNOMED CT and ICD-10-CM were built for different jobs. SNOMED CT is a clinical terminology — over 350,000 concepts, designed to capture what a clinician actually observed and thought, with fine-grained detail and a rich hierarchy of relationships between concepts. ICD-10-CM is a *classification* system — roughly 70,000 codes, designed to group cases into billing and statistical categories, not to capture every clinical nuance. A classification system, by design, sorts many distinct clinical realities into the same bucket when a finer distinction doesn't matter for its purpose (billing, population statistics) even though it might matter enormously for patient care.

Mapping between them is not a lookup table in the sense of a phone book, where each name has exactly one correct number. It's closer to translating between two languages that don't share the same concepts one-to-one — sometimes a mapping is clean and total, sometimes several source concepts collapse into one target code, and sometimes one source concept could legitimately map to several different target codes depending on information the mapping table itself doesn't have access to.

contentSections.scenario: A SNOMED CT concept for "acute myocardial infarction, ST elevation, of anterior wall" (a specific, detailed clinical concept) gets mapped, through the standard SNOMED-to-ICD map, to I21.9 — "ST elevation (STEMI) myocardial infarction of unspecified site."
contentSections.question: What happened to the anatomical detail ("anterior wall") in this mapping?

options.label: Nothing — I21.9 preserves it in a coded field the billing system reads separately

It was dropped — the target code collapses several site-specific STEMI concepts into one "unspecified site" code, and a more specific ICD-10-CM code (I21.0, anterior wall) existed but wasn't the one the mapping selected here
It was upgraded — ICD-10-CM has finer anatomical detail than SNOMED CT for cardiac events

feedback.preserved: There's no separate field carrying the anatomical detail forward — once the code selected is I21.9, the specific-site information isn't recoverable from the code itself. It would have to be re-derived by going back to the source SNOMED concept or the original note.
feedback.dropped: Right. ICD-10-CM does have a site-specific code available (I21.0, ST elevation myocardial infarction of anterior wall) — the loss here isn't that ICD-10-CM lacks the concept, it's that this particular mapping instance landed on the less specific code rather than the more specific one that was actually available and would have matched the source concept more precisely.
feedback.upgraded: ICD-10-CM's cardiac chapter does carry some site-specific codes, but nothing about this mapping upgraded anything — the specific detail present in the SNOMED source concept simply didn't make it into the code that was ultimately selected.

contentSections.concept: **A mapping doesn't fail by producing an invalid code — it fails, most often, by producing a valid code that's less specific than what the source documentation actually supports.** The information isn't corrupted; it's silently dropped, and a downstream reader of the code alone has no way to know it was ever there.

contentSections.title: Why the loss is where harm hides

contentSections.body: A registry study pulling ICD-10-CM codes to track site-specific STEMI outcomes for quality improvement can only see what the code says. If a real anterior-wall STEMI was mapped to I21.9 instead of I21.0, that case is invisible to any analysis filtering for I21.0 — not wrong, exactly, just gone from a dataset that depends on the code carrying detail it no longer carries.

The reason this module exists, and the reason mapping loss specifically deserves its own module rather than folding into the general "conformant but wrong" theme from modules one and two, is that lossy mapping is *structurally invisible in a different way* than the errors covered so far. A wrong-laterality code (module two) is checkable by comparing the code to the note — the information needed to catch it still exists in the record. A lossy mapping can drop information that was present in the *source* terminology but genuinely has no home in the *target* terminology's available codes for this case — meaning the check isn't "does this code match the note," it's "did a more specific target code exist that this mapping should have reached for instead." That requires knowing both terminologies well enough to know what the target *could* have said, not just what it does say.

This matters most exactly where it's least visible: quality metrics, population health tracking, prior-authorization decisions, and research datasets that all depend on code-level specificity that may have quietly evaporated somewhere in a mapping step nobody in the current pipeline chose deliberately — it was built into a general-purpose mapping table years earlier, by someone optimizing for a different use case.

contentSections.scenario: NLM's own published documentation for the SNOMED CT to ICD-10-CM map describes a substantial share of SNOMED CT concepts as mapping to an ICD-10-CM target with some kind of qualifying note, context-dependent rule, or "map with caution" flag, rather than a single unconditional direct target.
contentSections.question: Illustratively — of the SNOMED CT concepts covered by the standard US map, roughly what share carry some kind of context-dependent or rule-based mapping rather than a single, unconditional target code?
contentSections.explanation: This figure is illustrative, meant to convey scale rather than to be memorized — the real proportion varies by SNOMED CT hierarchy and changes with each map release. The point holds regardless of the exact number: a meaningful share of real-world mappings aren't simple one-to-one lookups at all, they're rule-based or context-dependent, which is exactly the terrain the next four lessons cover.

contentSections.body: Mapping between terminologies built for different jobs is inherently lossy — and the loss doesn't corrupt the code, it silently narrows it, in exactly the cases (quality tracking, research, prior auth) where the narrowed detail was the whole point.

title: One-to-many maps and the choice somebody made
description: When one source concept legitimately maps to several possible target codes depending on context the mapping table itself doesn't have — and how that ambiguity gets silently resolved, often by a default nobody chose on purpose for this specific case.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize a one-to-many mapping situation and the context it depends on
Identify when an automated pipeline likely defaulted rather than genuinely resolved a one-to-many map

contentSections.title: One concept, several legitimate targets

contentSections.body: SNOMED CT concept 22298006, "myocardial infarction," doesn't map to one ICD-10-CM code. Depending on information the SNOMED concept alone doesn't carry — is this ST-elevation or non-ST-elevation, is it a first occurrence or a subsequent one within the same episode of care, is it acute or being coded as a historical fact — the correct ICD-10-CM target could be I21.3, I21.4, I22.-, or Z95.5, among others. The mapping table has to resolve that somehow.

A **one-to-many map** is exactly this: one source concept, several legitimate ICD-10-CM targets, with the correct choice depending on context that lives in the note, not in the source code itself. The standard NLM map handles this with rule-based logic where possible ("if this additional finding is also present, use this target; otherwise use this default") — but rules can only fire on information that's actually present and structured in a machine-readable way. When the deciding context is buried in free text the pipeline didn't extract, or wasn't present as a discrete coded fact anywhere upstream, the mapping table falls back to a **default target** — its best general-purpose guess for the most common or least-committal case.

A default isn't a wrong answer by construction — it might be exactly right for this patient. It's a guess made by someone building a general-purpose mapping table, for the general case, without this specific patient's chart in front of them. Whether it happens to be right here is a separate question from whether it was chosen with this patient in mind, and it wasn't.

contentSections.scenario: An AI pipeline codes a chart documenting "NSTEMI, second episode this admission, on anticoagulation" and the resulting ICD-10-CM code is I21.4 (non-ST elevation MI) — correct — but confidence is reported as low, and a human reviewer notices the pipeline's internal mapping trace shows it fell back to a general default rather than resolving from a specific rule.
contentSections.question: Given that the final code happened to be correct, is there still something worth checking here?

options.label: No — the code is right, so nothing further matters

Yes — a correct result reached via a fallback default, rather than a rule that actually used this chart's specific context (second episode, on anticoagulation), is correct by coincidence for this case, and the same fallback could easily land on the wrong target for a superficially similar chart where the context differs
Yes, but only because the confidence score was low, which always means the code is wrong

feedback.no: The code being correct this one time doesn't tell you whether the mechanism that produced it is reliable — a fallback default that happened to match this chart isn't the same as a rule that actually used this chart's context, and the next chart with a similar shape but different context could easily get the same default wrongly.
feedback.yes: Right. A low-confidence, fallback-driven correct answer is worth noticing precisely because it reveals a mapping gap — this chart had exactly the context (second episode, anticoagulation) that should drive a more specific rule, and the pipeline didn't use it. That's useful information about the pipeline's blind spot even when today's specific chart came out fine.
feedback.conf: Low confidence is a signal worth investigating, not an automatic verdict either way — pair it with looking at *why* confidence was low (a fallback default, in this case) rather than treating the number alone as proof of anything.

contentSections.mechanism: **A one-to-many map resolved by a fallback default, rather than by a rule using the chart's actual context, produces a code that's right or wrong independent of whether the pipeline understood the case.** Spotting the fallback — even when the resulting code is correct — is how you find the exact place a pipeline is guessing well rather than reasoning well, before it guesses badly on a less typical chart.

contentSections.title: What the default is actually optimized for

contentSections.body: A default target in a general-purpose mapping table is usually chosen to be the most common case, the least clinically committal case, or simply whatever a mapping author decided was the safest generic answer years before this specific pipeline existed.

It's worth being specific about what a default is actually optimized for, because "default" sounds neutral and isn't. A mapping table author choosing a default target for an ambiguous SNOMED concept is typically optimizing for one of: the statistically most frequent scenario across a large population (which may not be this patient's scenario), the most conservative or least specific code available (safest in the sense of least likely to overstate severity, not necessarily most accurate), or simply an arbitrary but documented choice made to keep the mapping table complete. None of those three is "whatever actually happened to this patient," because the table's author never had this patient's chart. Recognizing when a code came from a default rather than a context-driven rule is the whole skill this lesson trains — and it usually shows up as a confidence dip, a mapping-trace flag if the pipeline exposes one, or simply a chart whose note contains exactly the kind of deciding detail (first vs. subsequent episode, with vs. without a named complication) that a rule *should* have used but the final code doesn't reflect.

contentSections.question: A chart documents a one-to-many SNOMED concept with clear deciding context in the note (e.g. "first occurrence," "with a named complication"), and the resulting code matches the general default rather than the context-specific target. What's the single fastest thing to check to confirm this was a fallback rather than a genuine judgment call?
contentSections.answer: Whether the pipeline's mapping trace (if exposed) shows a rule firing on that specific context, or a generic default path — and if no trace is available, whether the note's deciding detail is even structured/extracted anywhere the mapping logic could have used it. If the deciding fact never made it into a discrete, machine-readable field, a fallback was close to inevitable regardless of how clearly a human reading the note would have resolved it.
contentSections.hint: Ask not just what the final code is, but whether the specific deciding fact from the note was ever available to the mapping step in a form it could act on.

contentSections.body: A one-to-many map's default target is a general-purpose guess, not a judgment about this patient — noticing when a chart's own context should have driven a specific rule, and didn't, is how you catch a default that got lucky before it gets unlucky.

title: Granularity loss: the specific finding becoming a general one
description: When a mapping collapses several distinct, clinically meaningful source concepts into one broader target code — not because the target lacks the detail entirely, but because the mapping selected the broad code instead of the specific one that existed.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a case of granularity loss between a source finding and its mapped target code
Distinguish granularity loss (an available specific code not used) from a genuine terminology gap (no specific code exists)

contentSections.title: The specific finding, mapped to the general bucket

contentSections.body: A note documents "stage 3 chronic kidney disease, moderate, GFR 42 mL/min/1.73m², due to poorly controlled type 2 diabetes." The SNOMED concept captured is specific: diabetic nephropathy with CKD stage 3a. The AI-mapped ICD-10-CM code that lands on the claim is E11.9 — type 2 diabetes without complications. The complication documented, staged, and given a GFR value has vanished.

This is granularity loss in its most consequential shape: not a mapping that lacks a specific target, but a mapping that reached for the general one when a specific one existed and matched better. ICD-10-CM has E11.22 (type 2 diabetes with diabetic chronic kidney disease) and, separately, an N18.- series for CKD staging — the specificity exists in the target terminology. The failure is in the mapping step choosing E11.9 anyway, whether because the mapping logic weighted the more common "no complications" pattern more heavily, because the CKD staging information lived in a lab value the pipeline never connected back to the diabetes diagnosis, or because a lower-effort default fired instead of the rule that should have caught this connection.

Granularity loss matters clinically beyond the claim itself: E11.9 signals, to anyone reading the coded record later — a specialist, a care manager, a quality program — that this patient has uncomplicated diabetes. E11.22 signals ongoing kidney involvement requiring monitoring and specific medication caution (nephrotoxic drugs, contrast dye, dosing adjustments). The coded record isn't just a billing artifact here; for a patient whose next provider works partly from the coded history, it's part of how the complication gets remembered or forgotten.

contentSections.code:
Mapping trace excerpt (simplified):

Source: SNOMED 127013003 "Diabetic nephropathy"
  + SNOMED 431855005 "Chronic kidney disease stage 3a"
  + Observation: eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m2

Mapped target: E11.9
(Type 2 diabetes mellitus without complications)

Available alternative target: E11.22
(Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic chronic kidney disease)
+ N18.31 (Chronic kidney disease, stage 3a)
contentSections.question: What's the defect in this mapping, and is it a case of the target terminology lacking the needed detail?

options.label: No defect — E11.9 is a valid code and mapping to it isn't wrong

Granularity loss — E11.22 and the N18.31 CKD-staging code both exist and match the documented findings precisely; the mapping reached for the general "without complications" code instead of the specific ones that were available
A genuine terminology gap — ICD-10-CM has no way to represent diabetic CKD, so E11.9 was the best available option

feedback.none: E11.9 is a valid code in isolation, but "valid" isn't the question — the question is whether it's the best-matching code available, and it isn't: it directly contradicts the documented nephropathy and staged CKD finding by asserting "without complications."
feedback.loss: Right. Both E11.22 and N18.31 exist, are current, and match the source findings precisely. This is granularity loss in its clearest form — the target terminology had the specificity, and the mapping simply didn't reach it.
feedback.gap: There's no gap here — ICD-10-CM has a well-established, specific pathway for exactly this combination (diabetes-with-CKD codes plus CKD staging codes). If E11.9 were genuinely the only available option, that would be a different, rarer situation this lesson also covers, but it isn't the case here.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The tell in a mapping trace like this one is a source concept carrying real specificity (a named complication, a staged severity, a supporting lab value) landing on a target code whose own definition explicitly denies that specificity ("without complications"). When the source is specific and the target says the opposite of specific, that's granularity loss, not a coincidence of vocabulary.

contentSections.title: Loss versus a genuine gap

contentSections.body: Not every collapse into a broader code is granularity loss. A note documenting a rare, highly specific genetic variant of a condition may genuinely have no ICD-10-CM code that captures that level of detail — the classification system's granularity simply stops at a coarser level for that condition, and every coder, human or AI, faces the same ceiling.

Distinguishing genuine granularity loss from a real terminology gap matters because the fix is completely different. Granularity loss — the last example — is fixable by correcting the mapping to reach the specific code that already exists. A genuine gap has no such fix available at the coding level; the best a reviewer can do is code to the most specific available level and, where it matters clinically, ensure the missing nuance is preserved in the narrative documentation rather than expecting the code to carry it. Confusing the two leads in opposite unhelpful directions: treating a genuine gap as a mapping failure sends you looking for a specific code that doesn't exist, and treating real granularity loss as an unavoidable gap lets an actual mapping defect go uncorrected.

contentSections.scenario: Four coded records, each mapped to a broader code than the source clinical concept.
contentSections.question: Select every case that's actually a genuine terminology gap (no more specific target exists) rather than granularity loss (a specific target existed and wasn't used).

items.label: Diabetic nephropathy with staged CKD, mapped to E11.9 (from the earlier example)
A specific, rare genetic subtype of a metabolic disorder with no dedicated ICD-10-CM code, mapped to the disorder's general code
A documented right-wrist fracture mapped to the unspecified-laterality fracture code, when the right-side-specific code exists
A cluster of nonspecific symptoms without a settled diagnosis, mapped to the appropriate symptom-based R-code rather than a specific disease code

explanation.ckd: This is granularity loss, not a gap — E11.22 and the CKD staging codes both existed and matched the documentation.
explanation.rare-var: Correct — if ICD-10-CM genuinely has no code for the specific genetic subtype, coding to the general disorder code is the actual ceiling of what the classification allows, not a mapping failure.
explanation.fracture-side: This is granularity loss — a laterality-specific code existed and the note documented the side; nothing prevented the more specific code from being used.
explanation.symptom-cluster: Correct — coding a genuinely undiagnosed symptom cluster to an R-code (symptoms/signs) rather than inventing a more specific disease diagnosis the note doesn't support is actually the appropriate level of specificity, not a loss.

contentSections.synthesis: Two of the four are real mapping failures with an available fix; two are the classification system's actual limit, or appropriately conservative coding, where reaching for more specificity than the documentation supports would itself be an error in the other direction.

contentSections.body: Granularity loss is a specific, fixable failure — a more precise code existed and the mapping didn't reach it — and it's a different thing entirely from a genuine terminology gap, where no more specific code exists for anyone to reach.

title: Local codes, legacy systems, and the mapping table nobody owns
description: The mapping tables that never appear in any national standard — a hospital lab's internal test codes mapped to LOINC by whoever set up the interface years ago, unmaintained as methodology quietly changed underneath it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a local-to-standard code mapping table degrades over time even without anyone changing it
Identify signs that a local mapping table may be stale

contentSections.title: The mapping nobody's national standard covers

contentSections.body: A community hospital's lab system has run the same internal test code, "GLU1," for glucose since 2009, mapped at interface build time to LOINC 2345-7 (Glucose [Mass/volume] in Serum or Plasma). In 2018 the lab switched analyzers and, with them, switched from a serum-based to a plasma-based glucose assay — a real, if subtle, methodological change. The internal code GLU1 never changed. Neither did its mapping to LOINC 2345-7, even though the more precise LOINC code for the new method (2339-0, Glucose in Blood by Glucometer, or a different specific LOINC depending on the exact new method) may have been the more accurate target all along.

This is a different failure category from anything else in this module: there's no national standard to consult, no NLM map to audit, because **local codes** — a hospital's own internal identifiers for tests, procedures, or supplies that predate or sit alongside standard terminologies — are exactly that: local. Someone at this specific hospital, at some point, built a mapping table from GLU1 to a LOINC code, almost always as a one-time integration project. That mapping table then sits, unmaintained, while the underlying reality it describes — assay methodology, reference ranges, even what the test actually measures — can quietly change.

The mapping table doesn't announce its own staleness. It keeps working, in the narrow sense that messages keep flowing and codes keep resolving to something. What it stops doing, silently, is accurately describing what GLU1 currently means, because whoever owned that decision in 2009 is very possibly no longer at this hospital, and updating a working interface mapping is rarely anyone's current job description.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer notices that a hospital's glucose results, mapped through LOINC 2345-7, have reference ranges in the AI pipeline's output that look slightly off compared to what a modern serum glucose assay should show — and further digging finds the hospital switched its glucose analyzer and assay method five years ago.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely root mechanism?

options.label: The local-to-LOINC mapping table was built once, at initial integration, and was never revisited when the underlying lab methodology changed years later
LOINC itself changed its definition of code 2345-7 without notice
The AI pipeline is incapable of processing lab values correctly regardless of the mapping

feedback.stale: Right. This is the signature of a stale local mapping: the interface still runs, values still flow, but the mapping's own accuracy depends on an assumption (this hospital's current assay method) that quietly stopped being true when equipment or methodology changed, with no mechanism forcing anyone to revisit the mapping at that point.
feedback.loinc-changed: LOINC codes are versioned and occasionally deprecated, but a national terminology changing its own definitions is a different, much rarer event than a single hospital's unmaintained local mapping table falling out of sync with its own lab's methodology — and there's no indication here that LOINC itself changed anything.
feedback.ai-cant: The pipeline is processing exactly what the mapping table hands it — the defect is upstream, in what the local code has actually meant since the methodology change, not in the pipeline's ability to read a LOINC-coded value.

contentSections.mechanism: **A local mapping table is built once, against a snapshot of reality, and nothing about the interface itself forces a revisit when that reality changes.** Equipment swaps, assay method changes, and vendor updates all happen on their own schedule, entirely decoupled from whoever maintains — or, more often, doesn't maintain — the mapping table that translates a local code into a standard one.

contentSections.title: Signs a local mapping table is worth asking about

contentSections.body: You can't audit every local mapping table at every facility a pipeline touches — but certain signals are worth treating as a reason to ask, specifically, when a local code is involved.

A few practical tells: a reference range that looks slightly out of step with the modern standard for that test; a local code whose name suggests age or a superseded method ("GLU1" rather than a newer, more descriptive internal name, suggesting it predates a later system that never got it renamed); a facility that's undergone a known equipment, vendor, or EHR transition without a corresponding note of the mapping table being reviewed; and, most simply, no one at the facility being able to say when the local-to-standard mapping was last checked. None of these prove a stale mapping on their own — a slightly unusual reference range can have a dozen innocent explanations — but together, or even individually, they're worth a specific question rather than an assumption that a working interface is an accurate one.

contentSections.question: A local mapping table has been flagged as possibly stale, but you have no direct way to re-derive the correct current mapping yourself (you're not a lab methodologist). What's the realistic, honest next step?
contentSections.answer: Escalate a specific, answerable question to whoever owns the lab's current methodology — not "is this mapping wrong," but something concrete like "has the glucose assay method changed since this mapping was last set, and if so, does LOINC 2345-7 still correctly describe it." A reviewer's job here is surfacing the right question to the right person, not re-deriving lab science from first principles.
contentSections.hint: You don't need to be a lab methodologist to know a mapping might be stale — you need to know who to ask, and what specific, checkable question to ask them.

contentSections.body: A local mapping table has no national standard watching over it — it degrades silently as the reality underneath it changes, and a working interface is not the same claim as an accurate one.

title: Checking a map against the source, not the target
description: Closing the module: the discipline of verifying a mapped code by tracing back to what the source concept actually said, rather than judging the target code on its own terms — the one procedure that catches all three of this module's failure shapes.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a source-first verification procedure to a mapped code
Explain why checking a target code in isolation misses mapping errors that checking against the source catches

contentSections.title: Judging the target code alone tells you nothing about the mapping

contentSections.body: Handed just the final code — E11.9, on its own, with no source concept attached — there's nothing wrong with it to see. It's a real, current, correctly formatted code. Every failure this module has covered (a default that guessed wrong, a specific finding collapsed to a general one, a stale local mapping) is invisible if you only ever look at where the mapping landed.

This is the module's central procedural point, and it echoes module one's "conformant vs. correct" theme from a mapping-specific angle: **a mapped code can only be verified by comparing it back to its source concept, never by evaluating the target code in isolation.** The source concept — the SNOMED CT concept, the local lab code, the original clinical finding — is the only place the information needed to judge the mapping's accuracy actually lives. Once you're looking only at the ICD-10-CM or LOINC code that came out the other end, the comparison you'd need to make has nothing left to compare against.

In practice, this means the review habit to build is: don't start with the final code and ask "is this valid" — start with the source concept and ask "does this final code preserve everything about the source that a target code could have preserved." That single reframing catches one-to-many defaults that guessed wrong, granularity loss, and (where the mapping trace is available) stale local mappings, because all three are, structurally, the same question asked about a different part of the pipeline: what did the source actually say, and did the target keep it.

contentSections.problem: Source SNOMED concept: 90781000119102, "Diabetic peripheral angiopathy with gangrene, right foot." Mapped ICD-10-CM code on the claim: E11.51 (type 2 diabetes with diabetic peripheral angiopathy without gangrene). Verify the mapping.

steps.label: Read the source concept fully, not just its general category
steps.work: The SNOMED concept names three specific facts: diabetic peripheral angiopathy, WITH gangrene (not without), and right foot laterality.
steps.why: The source concept is the only place all three facts exist together — reading it in full, rather than skimming for the general diagnosis family, is what makes the rest of the check possible.

steps.label: Check whether the target code preserves each fact
steps.work: E11.51 captures diabetic peripheral angiopathy — correct family. But E11.51 specifically means "without gangrene" — the opposite of what the source documents. There's no laterality captured either, though ICD-10-CM's angiopathy-with-gangrene codes don't carry laterality distinctions the way injury codes do, so that specific omission may be an actual terminology limit rather than a mapping failure.
steps.why: Checking fact-by-fact, rather than accepting the general code family as "close enough," is what catches that the gangrene status was inverted, not just dropped.

steps.label: Identify the correct target and the nature of the error
steps.work: The correct code is E11.52 (type 2 diabetes with diabetic peripheral angiopathy WITH gangrene) — a real, available, more accurate target that the mapping should have reached instead of E11.51.
steps.why: This isn't granularity loss (a general code standing in for a specific one) — it's a more serious error: the mapped code asserts something that directly contradicts the source. Gangrene absent versus present is not a matter of specificity, it's a matter of the mapping getting the fact backwards.

faded.problem: Source SNOMED concept: 428281000, "Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute respiratory failure." Mapped code: J44.1 (COPD with acute exacerbation, no mention of respiratory failure captured separately, and no J96.- respiratory failure code present on the claim).

blanks.prompt: What specific fact from the source concept is missing from the mapped result?
blanks.why: The source concept explicitly names acute respiratory failure alongside the COPD exacerbation — a distinct, clinically significant complication that changes acuity and typically warrants its own code.

blanks.prompt: Is this a case of granularity loss, or the mapping asserting something that contradicts the source (like the gangrene example)?
accept: a specificity/granularity issue, not a contradiction
blanks.why: Unlike the gangrene case, J44.1 doesn't assert the opposite of respiratory failure — it simply omits it. The fix is adding the missing, available code (a J96.- respiratory failure code) rather than correcting an inverted fact.

blanks.prompt: What should the corrected code set include?
blanks.answer: j44.1 plus a j96 respiratory failure code
blanks.why: The COPD exacerbation code stays; a respiratory failure code needs to be added to capture the fact the source concept documents and the mapped result dropped.

contentSections.procedure: **Read the full source concept first → check whether the target preserves each individual fact, not just the general category → determine whether any gap is an omission (granularity loss), an inversion (a more serious error), or a genuine terminology limit.** Starting from the target code and working backward skips the one step — reading the source in full — that makes any of this possible.

contentSections.title: Closing the module

contentSections.body: Four lessons, one recurring shape: a source concept carries real information, a mapping step translates it into a different terminology built for a different purpose, and somewhere in that translation — a default that guessed at context it didn't have, a specific finding rounded up to a general bucket, a local table that stopped tracking a reality it once accurately described — something can go missing without the resulting code ever looking wrong on its own. The procedure this lesson closes on is the same procedure that runs through the whole module: don't evaluate the code you're handed. Trace it back to what it's supposed to represent, and check whether it still does.

contentSections.title: The gangrene mapping
contentSections.opening: You're reviewing the diabetic peripheral angiopathy claim from the worked example: source SNOMED concept documents gangrene present, right foot; mapped code E11.51 (without gangrene).

n1.situation: The claim, as coded, is ready to submit with E11.51. You have the full SNOMED source concept open beside it.
n1.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Approve — E11.51 is a valid, real code for diabetic peripheral angiopathy
choices.consequence: The claim submits asserting no gangrene is present, when the source clinical concept explicitly documents gangrene, right foot. Beyond the claim itself, this is now the coded record a future provider or care manager might read — materially understating this patient's severity and risk.

choices.label: Correct to E11.52 (with gangrene), citing the source SNOMED concept as the basis
choices.consequence: The corrected code now matches what the source concept actually documents, with a traceable reason.

choices.label: Glance at E11.51's own definition, confirm it's a real code, and move on without opening the source concept
choices.consequence: E11.51 looks completely fine in isolation — which is exactly the trap. Nothing about evaluating the target code alone would ever reveal that it contradicts the source.

good.summary: You traced the code back to its source concept and caught an inversion a target-only check would have missed entirely.
good.lesson: The target code was never going to reveal this error on its own — it took reading the source concept and checking fact by fact.

costly.summary: Evaluating the target code in isolation is structurally incapable of catching a mapping error, because the information needed for the comparison lives only in the source.
costly.lesson: This module's whole point: a mapped code can only be judged against its source, never on its own terms.

contentSections.body: A mapped code can only be verified by tracing it back to its source concept — evaluated on its own, every failure this module covers looks like nothing at all.

title: Assess eight mappings for meaning loss

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's mapping-verification checks to unfamiliar source/target pairs at speed
Distinguish genuine mapping loss from a real terminology gap or an appropriately general code

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across three — nothing here expires or times out.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Audit a mapping table for clinically significant loss
description: Given a set of source concepts and their mapped target codes, audit the mapping table for one-to-many defaults, granularity loss, and any signs of staleness — and write up each lossy mapping with its clinical consequence.

learningObjectives.text: Apply source-first verification systematically across a mapping table rather than one code at a time
Produce an audit naming the clinical consequence of each lossy mapping found

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: A mapping table looks like the most boring artifact in this whole pipeline — rows of source concepts and target codes. It's also exactly where the last four lessons' worth of failure modes live, all at once, waiting for someone to actually trace each row back to its source.

contentSections.title: Audit a mapping table for clinically significant loss
contentSections.brief: You're given a mapping table of fifteen rows: a source clinical concept (SNOMED CT or a local lab code) paired with its currently mapped target code (ICD-10-CM or LOINC). Some rows are accurate. Others contain a one-to-many default that ignored available context, granularity loss, or a plausible sign of local-mapping staleness. Audit the table and name each lossy mapping's clinical consequence.
contentSections.deliverable: An audit listing all fifteen rows: for each, either 'accurate mapping, because ___' or a specific finding naming the failure type, what the source actually documented, what the target should have been (where a correction exists), and the clinical consequence of the loss.

stages.title: Build the mapping table
stages.instructions: Write fifteen source-concept-to-target-code rows spanning at least three different clinical areas (e.g. diabetes complications, cardiac events, infections, renal disease). Seed at least eight rows with a genuine issue — mix of one-to-many defaults that ignored available context, granularity loss, and at least one plausible local-mapping-staleness scenario — plus at least three genuinely accurate rows and at least one genuine terminology-gap row (correctly coded to the most specific available level, not actually an error). Keep a private answer key.
stages.checkpoint: You have fifteen rows spanning at least three clinical areas, with at least eight seeded issues across multiple failure types, at least three accurate rows, one genuine-gap row, and a private answer key.

stages.title: Audit each row source-first
stages.instructions: Set the answer key aside. For each row, read the full source concept before looking at whether the target preserves it. Classify each row as accurate, a specific failure type with a named correction, or a genuine terminology gap. Write the clinical consequence for every row you flag as a real issue — what would a clinician, a quality program, or a future coder miss because of this specific loss.
stages.checkpoint: All fifteen rows have a classification and, for flagged rows, a stated clinical consequence grounded in what was actually lost.

stages.title: Self-check against your answer key
stages.instructions: Compare against your answer key. Which seeded issues did you catch, across which failure types? Did you correctly leave the genuine-gap row uncorrected rather than inventing a fix for it? Did you flag any accurate row incorrectly?
stages.checkpoint: You know which issues you caught and missed, handled the genuine-gap row correctly, and corrected any false flags on accurate rows.

rubric.criterion: Every row was checked source-first, not target-first
rubric.meets: The audit shows evidence of reading each source concept in full before judging its target, for every row, not just the ones that turned out flagged.

rubric.criterion: Findings span more than one failure type
rubric.meets: The audit reflects catching one-to-many defaults, granularity loss, and at least a plausible staleness case as genuinely distinct findings, not all one pattern.

rubric.criterion: The genuine terminology-gap row is correctly left uncorrected
rubric.meets: The audit recognizes the gap row as the classification ceiling it is, rather than inventing a nonexistent 'more specific' code for it.

rubric.criterion: Each flagged finding states a real clinical consequence, not just 'this is technically imprecise'
rubric.meets: Every finding explains what a clinician, quality program, or future coder would actually miss or misunderstand because of this specific loss.

rubric.criterion: The self-check honestly accounts for what was missed
rubric.meets: The write-up names any seeded issue that was missed and which part of the source-first procedure would have caught it.

contentSections.body: A mapping table's rows all look equally clean until you trace each one back to its source — the audit is the discipline of actually doing that, row by row, instead of trusting that a working table is an accurate one.

questions.from: This module — Mapping is lossy
questions.prompt: Why is mapping between SNOMED CT and ICD-10-CM inherently prone to loss?

options.label: The two terminologies were built for different purposes at different levels of granularity — a clean one-to-one correspondence isn't guaranteed
SNOMED CT is a less reliable terminology than ICD-10-CM
Mapping software is inherently less accurate than manual coding

questions.explanation: This is a structural fact about the two systems' differing purposes and granularity, not a reliability judgment about either terminology or about mapping software generally.

questions.from: This module — One-to-many maps
questions.prompt: A one-to-many map's fallback default produces a correct code for this patient by coincidence. Is there still something worth noting?

options.label: Yes — a fallback that happened to be right this time didn't use this chart's actual context, and could misfire on a similar chart with different context
No — a correct result means the mechanism is reliable
Only if the confidence score was low

questions.explanation: Correctness this time doesn't establish reliability — the fallback ignored context that should have driven a specific rule, and the same gap could misfire on the next similar chart.

questions.from: This module — Granularity loss
questions.prompt: What distinguishes granularity loss from a genuine terminology gap?

options.label: Granularity loss means a more specific target code existed and wasn't used; a genuine gap means no more specific code exists at all
They require the identical fix
Granularity loss only happens with local codes, never with national terminologies

questions.explanation: The presence or absence of an available, more specific code is exactly what separates a fixable mapping failure from the classification system's actual ceiling.

questions.from: This module — Checking a map against the source
questions.prompt: Why can't a mapped code's accuracy be verified by evaluating the target code alone?

options.label: The information needed for the comparison — what the source concept actually documented — only exists on the source side, not in the target code itself
Target codes are never valid on their own
It can be verified from the target alone, given enough terminology expertise

questions.explanation: A comparison needs both sides — without the source concept, there's nothing to compare the target against, no matter how expert the reviewer is.

questions.from: Previous module — Structurally Complete, Clinically Wrong
questions.prompt: What does a claims-edit engine's "zero errors" result actually verify?

options.label: Structural well-formedness and known payer combination rules — not that codes match the source note
That a human has confirmed medical necessity
That the claim will definitely be paid

questions.explanation: Same distinction as this module's source-verification theme, one layer up the pipeline: passing an automated check is a narrower claim than being correct.

questions.prompt: What determines which diagnosis is sequenced as principal on an inpatient claim?

options.label: The condition, after study, chiefly responsible for occasioning the admission
Whichever condition is generally most severe
Whichever condition was documented first

questions.explanation: Sequencing follows what actually drove the admission, not general severity or documentation order.

options.label: Each code passes its own individual checks; the contradiction only exists in comparing the two codes' definitions against each other
Contradictory codes are always structurally invalid on their own
Payers never write edits for any combination

questions.explanation: Both codes in a contradictory pair are typically individually valid — the contradiction only exists in their relationship, which a per-code check doesn't compare.

They're the same failure mode
Implausibility only applies to obstetric records

That every value has been clinically verified
