learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's compliance checks to unfamiliar coded encounters at speed
Distinguish a genuine compliance risk from a properly supported code

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across three — nothing here expires or times out.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Write clinician queries for five ambiguous encounters
description: Given five encounters where documentation genuinely doesn't resolve a coding question, write five non-leading, clinically grounded queries that would stand up in an audit — and self-check each against the compliant-query standard from this module.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish genuine documentation ambiguity from a reviewer's own uncertainty across a set of real encounters
Produce non-leading, clinically grounded, multi-option queries for genuinely ambiguous documentation

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Five real-shaped ambiguities, five queries that have to do actual work — cite the specific indicators, stay open to more than one answer, and never tip toward the code that happens to reimburse better.

contentSections.title: Write clinician queries for five ambiguous encounters
contentSections.brief: You're given (or will construct) five encounter notes where the documentation genuinely supports more than one reasonable coding outcome, spanning different clinical areas (e.g. an acuity question like the anemia example, a specificity question like the pneumonia example, a causality question, a laterality-adjacent ambiguity, and one of your own design). For each, confirm the ambiguity is genuine, then write a compliant query.
contentSections.deliverable: Five encounter notes paired with five compliant queries, each query citing specific documented indicators, presenting genuinely open multiple options, and asking for the clinician's own judgment rather than confirmation of a stated answer.

stages.title: Build five genuinely ambiguous encounters
stages.instructions: Write five short encounter notes (4-8 sentences each) spanning different clinical areas, each containing clinical indicators that genuinely support more than one reasonable coding outcome — not a case where the answer is actually clear if you look closely, and not a case with no clinical indicators at all (which wouldn't be answerable by any query). For each, note privately what the two or more reasonable outcomes are and why the documentation doesn't settle between them.
stages.checkpoint: You have five notes across different clinical areas, each with genuine, defensible ambiguity between at least two reasonable coding outcomes, and a private note on what those outcomes are.

stages.title: Draft a compliant query for each
stages.instructions: For each encounter, write a query that cites the specific clinical indicators from that note, presents the genuinely reasonable options without indicating a preferred answer, and asks for the clinician's own clinical judgment. Avoid stating a suspected diagnosis and asking for confirmation.
stages.checkpoint: Five drafted queries, each grounded in that encounter's specific documented findings and offering genuinely open options.

stages.title: Self-check each query against the compliant-query standard
stages.instructions: Reread each query and check it against the three properties from this module: does it cite specific clinical indicators (not a vague request), does it present multiple genuinely reasonable options (not one option dressed as a question), and does it ask for the clinician's own judgment (not confirmation of a stated conclusion)? Revise any query that fails a property.
stages.checkpoint: All five queries satisfy all three properties, with at least one query revised as a result of this check.

rubric.criterion: All five encounters reflect genuine documentation ambiguity, not a reviewer-skill gap or an unanswerable case
rubric.meets: Each note contains clinical indicators supporting at least two reasonable outcomes, with a private note explaining what those outcomes are and why the record doesn't resolve between them.

rubric.criterion: Each query cites specific clinical indicators from its own note
rubric.meets: No query is generic — each references the actual findings, values, or documented details from its paired encounter.

rubric.criterion: Each query presents genuinely open, multiple reasonable options
rubric.meets: No query states a single suspected diagnosis and asks only for confirmation — each offers at least two real options without signaling a preferred answer.

rubric.criterion: Each query asks for the clinician's own clinical judgment
rubric.meets: The phrasing asks the clinician to determine or specify, not to confirm or verify a stated conclusion.

rubric.criterion: The self-check produced at least one genuine revision
rubric.meets: At least one of the five queries was revised as a result of checking it against the three-property standard, not simply confirmed as already correct.

contentSections.body: A compliant query is exactly as much work as a correct code — cite what's actually documented, stay genuinely open to more than one answer, and ask the person whose judgment actually resolves it.

options.label: No — it's defined by the gap between the code and the documented/actual reality, regardless of intent
Yes, by definition
Only for chronic-condition codes, not procedure codes

questions.explanation: Upcoding is defined by the code-versus-reality mismatch, not by anyone's state of mind — which is exactly why a pipeline with no intent at all can produce it.

questions.from: This module — Unbundling and the modifier that shouldn't be there
questions.prompt: Does a claim processing successfully with modifier 59 attached prove the modifier's factual claim (genuinely separate site/session/procedure) was true?

options.label: No — successful processing means the claim didn't trip an automated edit, not that the underlying factual claim was verified
Yes — payer systems verify modifier justifications before processing
Only for claims involving orthopedic procedures

questions.explanation: This is exactly why modifier 59 is a frequent post-payment audit target — pre-submission processing checks structural rules, not whether the documentation actually supports the distinct-service claim.

questions.from: This module — Documentation that doesn't support the code billed
questions.prompt: What does the MEAT standard actually require for coding a chronic condition at a given encounter?

options.label: The condition must be Monitored, Evaluated, Assessed, or Treated at that specific encounter — not simply present on the active problem list
The condition must appear somewhere in the patient's chart history
The condition must be confirmed by a specialist

questions.explanation: A condition being real and chronic elsewhere in the chart doesn't satisfy MEAT — the specific encounter being coded has to show one of the four elements.

questions.from: This module — Query the clinician
questions.prompt: What makes a clinician query non-compliant ("leading")?

options.label: It states the desired answer and asks only for confirmation, rather than presenting genuinely open multiple options
It cites specific clinical indicators from the note
It's shorter than three sentences

questions.explanation: Citing specific indicators is actually a required property of a good query; what makes a query leading is stating one desired answer and asking only for confirmation, rather than offering genuinely open options.

questions.from: Previous module — HIPAA, Minimum Necessary and Real Privacy
questions.prompt: Why can a record with every Safe Harbor identifier field removed still be re-identifying?

options.label: Free text can contain a combination of ordinary-sounding details that narrows to one identifiable person, with nothing flagged as an identifier field
Safe Harbor's field list is incomplete
It can't — full field compliance always guarantees de-identification

questions.explanation: The re-identifying information can live entirely in free text, invisible to a check that only looks at labeled identifier fields.

questions.from: Previous module — HIPAA, Minimum Necessary and Real Privacy
questions.prompt: Does minimum necessary apply to a specialist receiving a full chart for a treatment referral?

options.label: No — treatment-purpose disclosures are explicitly exempt
Yes, the same as any other disclosure
Only within the same health system

questions.explanation: The treatment exception is a deliberate, explicit carve-out specifically so clinical care isn't compromised by an artificial data trim.

questions.from: Previous module — HIPAA, Minimum Necessary and Real Privacy
questions.prompt: Does a signed BAA automatically authorize a vendor to use PHI for training its own general-purpose model?

options.label: No — that's a distinct use requiring its own explicit authorization
Yes, any signed BAA covers any use
Only for large, well-known vendors

questions.explanation: A BAA defines specific permitted purposes — model training for the vendor's own broader product is a materially different use needing its own explicit authorization.

questions.from: Two modules back — Terminology Mapping and Its Traps
questions.prompt: What distinguishes granularity loss from a genuine terminology gap?

options.label: Granularity loss means a more specific code existed and wasn't used; a genuine gap means none exists at all
They require the identical response
Granularity loss only occurs with local codes

questions.explanation: Whether a more specific target code is actually available is what separates a correctable mapping failure from the classification system's real ceiling.

questions.from: Two modules back — Terminology Mapping and Its Traps
questions.prompt: Why can't a mapped code's accuracy be verified by evaluating the target code alone?

options.label: The information needed for the comparison — what the source concept documented — only exists on the source side
Target codes are never valid on their own
It can be verified from the target alone with enough expertise

questions.explanation: A comparison needs both sides — without the source concept, there's nothing to compare the target code against.

questions.from: This module — Audit trails: making your own review defensible
questions.prompt: Does a system log showing a reviewer clicked "approve," with a timestamp, prove a genuine review took place?

options.label: No — a genuine review and a rubber-stamp approval produce the identical log entry; only the reviewer's own documented reasoning distinguishes them
Yes — the timestamp itself is proof of due diligence
Only if the reviewer has a strong track record

questions.explanation: This closes the phase on the same note it opened on: a surface artifact — here, an approval log — has to be traced back to what actually supports it, and a bare action log doesn't capture that.

contentSections.body: This closes the phase: five modules, one recurring question asked of a standard, a validator, a mapping, a privacy claim, and finally your own review record — does the surface artifact actually match what it claims to represent.
